en: Having bowed to those Arhats by whose illustrious names success in all desired fortunes may be attained, I compose this commentary on the *Kaṅkāla-adhyāya*. 1.1.

Having heard something from my gurus, having combined some [teachings] with those of the knowers of reality, and having experienced something for myself as well, this treatise is now being explained by me. (Radhy 1.2)
(On the importance of personal observation:
Even if taught directly by the Guru, alchemy does not succeed as long as the ritual procedure has not been witnessed two or three times in the presence of the Guru. (Radhy 1.3)
Therefore, having heard this or even seeing it anywhere else,
fools who nevertheless expend their wealth suffer in vain.
If the true guru, having become gracious, should demonstrate all the rites even in play, then all yogas will undoubtedly be accomplished. (Radhy 1.5)

Therefore, even when the meaning of the text has been clearly stated here, one should not exert effort in the practice of alchemy (*dhātuvāda*), disregarding the Guru, because of the lack of primary certainty. (Radhy 1.6)
He who speaks does not know; he who knows does not speak.
Therefore, wise men should not extend their mouths [to speak] anywhere at all.
Skilled in elixirs, pills, and collyria, he became worthy of the illustrious Kaṅkālaya;
by him, for the sake of instructing his own disciples, the true nature of mercury was revealed. (Radhy 1.8)
The virtuous disciple of Śrī Kaṅkālaya, for the benefit of himself and others, has composed this *Rasādhyāya* consisting of twenty-one chapters.
*Rasādhyāyaṭīkā*: [Commentary on the *Rasādhyāya*]
In this regard, at the very outset, he states the salutation to the chosen deity for the sake of accomplishing the task undertaken without obstacles.
Having first prostrated before the illustrious Bhairava, the omniscient Lord of the three worlds, I salute the illustrious Bhāratī and Vighneśa for the pacification of obstacles. (Radhy 1.10)

Celibacy, austerity, and the eating of sacrificial food must be practiced; [these] do not succeed when ritual action has failed, nor do they bear fruit when austerity is lost. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) consists of avoiding sexual intercourse with women. Austerity (*tapas*) is the performance of various forms of bodily mortification. "Eating sacrificial food" means consuming food that is fit for offerings. These practices do not lead to success when one has fallen away from ritual action (*kriyā*), nor do they yield results when austerity has been destroyed. Ritual action refers to the performance of rites such as bathing, fire-offerings, and circumambulation. Austerity refers to the endurance of hardships such as standing in water, fasting, and exposure to heat or cold. Even if these are performed, they do not bring about the desired goal if one has deviated from the prescribed ritual procedures. Furthermore, even if ritual action is correctly performed, it does not bear fruit if the mind is distracted by worldly objects or if the senses are agitated by passion. Therefore, one should practice celibacy, austerity, and the consumption of sacrificial food while remaining steadfast in ritual action and maintaining the power of austerity. Only then do they lead to the attainment of the supreme state. Otherwise, they are merely empty exertions. Thus it is said: "The wise man should always perform his duties with a focused mind; otherwise, he will wander through the cycle of rebirth. *Rasādhyāyaṭīkā*. 1.11. End of Chapter One. *Rasādhyāya*. In this [work], there are eighty-four alchemical operations (rasakarma), eighty-four varieties of pills (guṭikā), and eighty-four collyriums (añjana).
Thus, there are two hundred and fifty-two such divisions.

Therefore, from among these various types [of rites], when any one particular rite is commenced, then for one month prior to its commencement, austerity in the form of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) must be practiced;
this is because celibacy alone is the root of all austerity.
Because everything else, including austerity, is fruitless for one who is devoid of that [faith].
Or rather, celibacy (brahmacarya) should be maintained.
Thus, austerity should be performed by the teacher and others according to what is appropriate.
Because both are the primordial root of all karmic fruits.
Likewise, one should prepare sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) mixed with ghee and sugar, as well as milk-rice (pāyasa) and a meal of milk.
Because there is no purification of the body through other types of food.
And because of the absence of the means for breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Therefore, while thus maintaining one's duty, one must carry through to its conclusion the fruit of that action.
For this reason, when the practitioner has failed—meaning when he does not consume the food as prescribed—the ritual actions beginning with the extraction of the *rasa* do not succeed.
And when austerity has perished, they do not bear fruit.
And he himself will clarify this at the end of the book.
Now begins the chapter of the illustrious Kaṅkālayayogin,
wherein I shall speak of the flavor of the chain (*śṛṅkhalā-rasa*) as it is manifested through logical arguments.
Commentary on the *Rasādhyāya-ṭīkā*:
"I shall speak of the chapter that has come from the presence of the venerable Kaṅkālaya-yogin"—this is the statement of the disciple. (RadhyT 1.12:1)
In this chapter, the flavor of the chain (śṛṅkhalā-rasa) has been revealed through logical arguments and procedures such as medicinal saturation (bhāvanā), fire-purification (puṭa), and so forth.
Just as a chain is connected through the mutual interpenetration of its successive links, so it is here as well.
First, the purification of mercury.
Then follows the process of reviving the swooned purified mercury.
The casting down of one who has been raised up from a swoon. // RadhyT_1.12:6 //
And the restoration of one who has fallen [from his status]. RadhyT 1.12:7.
Fomentation for one who has been cast down and raised up.
And for one who has been fomented by sweating, there is the state of being restrained.
The state of being a restrainer belongs to that which has been directed. 1.12:10.
And the stretching out of what has been contracted. // RadhyT 1.12:11 //
And the digestion of mica for one who has extended his limbs in a crooked posture.
And the digestion of iron by means of aged abhraka.
And there is the digestion of rusted iron by means of the streaks shining like steel.
And by means of a king who has the luster of worn iron, there is the digestion of gold-king.
The digestion of sulfur by means of aged gold-leaf.
And the digestion of the essence of realgar by means of aged sulphur.
And the digestion of copper essence by means of the essence of decayed stone.
And the digestion of iron-sattva that has been worn out by the path of food and diamonds.
And the binding of the worn-out vajra.
The stretching of the bindu. RadhyT 1.12:21.
And the killing of one who has been brought back [to life].
And there is the transference of that which has been killed.
And there is bondage for one who has been made to step [over the fire].
And the untying of the bond.
Thus. RadhyT 1.12:26.
Thus, the reality is that the subsequent impression (*saṃskāra*) is knotted to the preceding impression of the flavor (*rasa*); it is for this reason that it is so called. RadhyT 1.12:27.

Next, I shall describe the defects of mercury (*sūta*), purification prior to its refinement (*saṃskāra*), the fruits of the mercurial elixirs (*rasa*), their origin, and the alchemy for the body and metals. Radhy 1.13. @------------------
Commentary on the Chapter on Mercury: The twelve defects of mercury (pārada).
I shall first describe the eighteen refinements, such as *pāṭasāraṇā* and others, by means of which one attains purity and stainlessness through the removal of those defects.
Then follows the fruit, which consists of the production of the *tāra* and other [refinements] from the refined essences (*rasa*).
Then [he perceives] the production of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as copper, tin, lead, and so forth.
"Therefore, I shall speak of the alchemy for perfecting the body and the alchemy for perfecting iron," said the disciple of Śrīkaṅkālaya.
Here, he states the answer to the proposition in due order.

One is the earthen coating, and two are the stone coatings.

The five colors are as follows: *śyāmā* (darkish), *kālikā* (blackish), and *kṛṣṇavarṇikā* (black-colored). These seven innate (*sahaja*) coatings (*kañcuka*) are always produced from mercury. *Commentary: Rasādhyāyaṭīkā:* The five colors are: *śyāmā*, *kālikā*, *kṛṣṇavarṇikā*, *nīlā*, and *pītā*. These seven innate coatings are always produced from mercury. They are called "innate" because they arise simultaneously with the [birth of] mercury. The seven coatings are: *mala*, *malina*, *tāra*, *kṛṣṇa*, *nīla*, *pīta*, and *rakta*. Among these, *mala* is the first coating; it is like the color of a pigeon's wing and is very difficult to remove. *Malina* is the second coating; it is like the color of a crow's beak and is slightly more easily removed than the first. *Tāra* is the third coating; it is like the color of a blue lotus and is easily removed. *Kṛṣṇa* is the fourth coating; it is like the color of black collyrium and is easily removed. *Nīla* is the fifth coating; it is like the color of a sapphire and is easily removed. *Pīta* is the sixth coating; it is like the color of turmeric and is easily removed. *Rakta* is the seventh coating; it is like the color of vermilion and is easily removed. Thus, these seven innate coatings are described. One should know that there are also seven acquired (*āgantuka*) coatings, which are produced by external causes such as heat, cold, and so forth. They are: *dhūmra*, *kapila*, *lohita*, *harita*, *pīta*, *śveta*, and *śyāma*. Among these, *dhūmra* is the first acquired coating; it is like the color of smoke and is easily removed. *Kapila* is the second acquired coating; it is like the color of a tawny cow and is easily removed. *Lohita* is the third acquired coating; it is like the color of red lead and is easily removed. *Harita* is the fourth acquired coating; it is like the color of green grass and is easily removed. *Pīta* is the fifth acquired coating; it is like the color of gold and is easily removed. *Śveta* is the sixth acquired coating; it is like the color of a conch shell and is easily removed. *Śyāma* is the seventh acquired coating; it is like the color of a dark cloud and is easily removed. Thus, the seven acquired coatings are described. One should know that there are also seven secret (*guhya*) coatings, which are produced by the power of mantras and medicinal herbs. They are: *vajra*, *ratna*, *loha*, *tāra*, *suvarṇa*, *rūpya*, and *tāmra*. Among these, *vajra* is the first secret coating; it is like the hardness of a diamond and is very difficult to remove. *Ratna* is the second secret coating; it is like the hardness of a gemstone and is very difficult to remove. *Loha* is the third secret coating; it is like the hardness of iron and is very difficult to remove. *Tāra* is the fourth secret coating; it is like the hardness of silver and is very difficult to remove. *Suvarṇa* is the fifth secret coating; it is like the hardness of gold and is very difficult to remove. *Rūpya* is the sixth secret coating; it is like the hardness of white metal and is very difficult to remove. *Tāmra* is the seventh secret coating; it is like the hardness of copper and is very difficult to remove. Thus, the seven secret coatings are described. One should know that there are also seven supreme (*uttama*) coatings, which are produced by the power of the Great Accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*). They are: *amṛta*, *sudhā*, *rasāyana*, *vajra*, *ratna*, *loha*, and *tāra*. Among these, *amṛta* is the first supreme coating; it is like nectar and is impossible to remove. *Sudhā* is the second supreme coating; it is like ambrosia and is impossible to remove. *Rasāyana* is the third supreme coating; it is like an elixir and is impossible to remove. *Vajra* is the fourth supreme coating; it is like a diamond and is impossible to remove. *Ratna* is the fifth supreme coating; it is like a gemstone and is impossible to remove. *Loha* is the sixth supreme coating; it is like iron and is impossible to remove. *Tāra* is the seventh supreme coating; it is like silver and is impossible to remove. Thus, the seven supreme coatings are described. One should know that there are also seven inferior (*adhama*) coatings, which are produced by the power of ignorance and lack of practice. They are: *mala*, *malina*, *tāra*, *kṛṣṇa*, *nīla*, *pīta*, and *rakta*. Among these, *mala* is the first inferior coating; it is like dirt and is easily removed. *Malina* is the second inferior coating; it is like grime and is easily removed. *Tāra* is the third inferior coating; it is like tarnish and is easily removed. *Kṛṣṇa* is the fourth inferior coating; it is like blackness and is easily removed. *Nīla* is the fifth inferior coating; it is like blueness and is easily removed. *Pīta* is the sixth inferior coating; it is like yellowness and is easily removed. *Rakta* is the seventh inferior coating; it is like redness and is easily removed. Thus, the seven inferior coatings are described. One should know that there are also seven neutral (*madhyama*) coatings, which are produced by the power of mixed causes. They are: *dhūmra*, *kapila*, *lohita*, *harita*, *pīta*, *śveta*, and *śyāma*. Thus, the seven neutral coatings are described. One should know that there are also seven ultimate (*parama*) coatings, which are produced by the power of the ultimate reality. And here, those things which are seen within water due to its contact with earth, stone, or other water, as well as those on the surface of milk and so forth, are called *kañcukas*.
Furthermore, the distinction is that those [faults] which become intoxicating in *kodrava* grains are the specific defects.
Now, he describes the specific transformations of each of these defects.
From the clay-based *kañcuka*, leprosy arises in embodied beings. (Radhy 1.18)
From stone arises dullness (*jāḍya*), and from water arises a mass of wind; these two produce *cilharī* in the body, as well as tin, lead, and bone-fragments. (Radhy 1.19)
Kālikā always causes elephantiasis, ringworm, jaundice, as well as delusion, indigestion, and jaundice (kāmalā). (Radhy 1.20)
White leprosy arises from the husk of *śyāmāka* grain;
the impurity produced from mercury destroys the vital energy of the body.
Fire causes the destruction of living beings and produces poisonous smoke;
through pride, one's limb indeed bursts asunder, and from madness, further madness arises.
If one should give mercury that is joined with the twelve defects,
for him there shall always be the sins of killing, such as the murder of a Brahmin.
He who gives the Lord of Mercury (Pārada), freed from the twelve defects,

Freed from the twelve defects and processed with refinements numbering the continents, mercury makes the body free from disease and acts as a metal for the body. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* The term "deha" refers to mercury (*rasa*). Mercury, when liberated from the twelve defects and refined by the eighteen purificatory processes (*saṃskāra*), renders the body free from disease and serves as a metallic elixir for the body. The "twelve defects" are: *mala*, *viṣa*, *vahnimāndya*, *mandakāritva*, *svedana*, *chedana*, *bhedana*, *dāha*, *mūrchana*, *utthāpana*, *śoṣaṇa*, and *māraṇa*. The "eighteen purificatory processes" are: *mardana*, *mūrchana*, *utthāpana*, *pātana*, *niyāmana*, *dīpana*, *cāraṇa*, *garbhadruti*, *bāhyadruti*, *jāraṇa*, *rāga*, *krāmaṇa*, *vedha*, *dhānyābhra*, *mūṣābandha*, *koṣṭhikābandha*, *drāvaṇa*, and *māraṇa*. By means of these, mercury becomes capable of transforming the body into a metallic state. Thus ends the twenty-fifth verse of the first chapter, the *Rasādhyāya*.
All eight verses are indeed clear; the only point requiring clarification is that *cilharī* is simply a specific variety of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
Thus ends the exposition on the defects and qualities of the charioteer.
START Radhy 1.26–30 (The eighteen purificatory processes): In this [chapter], there are eighteen purificatory processes (*saṃskāras*); among them, the first is *pāṭasāraṇa*.
The second is named Mardana, and the third is considered to be Śodhana.
The fourth is the awakening of the mercury; the fifth is the precipitation of the essence;
the sixth is the re-extraction of the essence; and the seventh is the sweating. (Radhy 1.27)
The eighth is declared the director (niyāmaka), while the ninth is the restrainer (nirodhaka).
The tenth should be the opener (mukhakārī), and the one numbered eleven (rudra) is indeed the digester (jāraṇa).
Sūryāṅka is said to be a binder; Sāraṇa is situated among the yakṣas;
Māraṇa shall consist of the number of humans (fourteen); and Pratisāraṇa has the lunar days (fifteen) as its mark.

The sixteenth stage is *krāmaṇa* (transference), the seventeenth is *vedha* (piercing), and the eighteenth is *saṃskāra* (refinement); by those who know it, this is considered *udghāṭana* (unveiling). (Radhy 1.30) [Commentary: Rasādhyāyaṭīkā] The sixteenth stage is *krāmaṇa*, which consists of the transference of the mercury (*rasa*) from the crucible (*kuṇḍalinī*) into the *mūlādhāra*. The seventeenth is *vedha*, which is the piercing of the *nāḍīs* by means of the *vīrya* (potency) of the mercury. The eighteenth is *saṃskāra*, which is the purification of the mercury; this is known as *udghāṭana* by the experts. It is said that when the mercury is thus purified, it becomes capable of entering the body and acting as a catalyst for transformation. Thus ends the first chapter on the stages of mercury.
The five verses are clear. *Ratnagotravibhāga* 1.26–30.1.
These are the eighteen purificatory rites for the charioteer.
Then, explaining the formative forces (saṃskāra) in their proper order, he says:
START Radhy 1.31 (pāṭasāraṇa):
When the molten metal has been strained through a cloth, that purification process is called *pāṭasāraṇa*.
All impurities, such as tin, lead, and the like, remain caught in the cloth.
*Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):

To cause [the horse] to abandon its blackness, a clod of earth should be applied from the side of the charioteer.
And one pala of that [mercury] along with sixty-four palas of lead.

Having combined one *pala* of well-prepared white *loṣṭajīkaka* with sixty-four *palas* of mercury, one should place both in a mortar and grind them for one *prahara*. And by means of that juice, for seven days, [the substance] ground [with it] becomes encased in water (*ambukañcuka*).
Commentary on the *Rasādhyāya*:

The *kāpālī* [impurity] arising from tin (*vaṅga*) is removed when it has been ground with a decoction of *citraka*.

The impurities (*kañcuka*) of mercury are destroyed by means of flour over seven times seven days.

Merely with the juice of those three—vajra, the root of snuhī, and śūraṇa—[one attains success].

All coatings, moreover, are destroyed by the rubbing of the mercury for seven days with the aforementioned liquid.

The fault of pride does not perish by being ground with the juice of the *nāhya* plant;

START *Radhy* 1.43–46 (mūrchana):
Crushed natural mercury, purified with a decoction of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), [is used].
And likewise with the juice of fresh ginger and the juice of fresh *ārdraka*.
In this manner, with the juice of *kākamācī* and the juice of *devadālī*, one should repeatedly grind what has dried and dry it again, rubbing and drying it over and over. (Radhy 1.44)
At the conclusion of each medicinal substance, one should wash it with fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika);

(Reviving): The reviving of the swooning mercury must be performed with five medicinal substances;

Mercury purified according to the previous method should first be ground with a decoction of *trikaṭu* in a mortar for seven days as before, and then dried. (RadhyT 1.43–46:1)
Thereafter, it should be washed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
In this manner, with the juice of the *bhūmidūdhelī* plant, and then with the fresh juice [of other plants].
Thereafter, with the essence of the ritual action.
Afterwards, with the juice of *devadālī*.
Having crushed it for seven days at a time and dried it, it should be washed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
When this has been done, that [substance], having risen from its swoon, is called pārada and becomes radiant.
Thus ends the fourth [chapter], the refinement for reviving one who has fainted.

When the mercury, having abandoned its dense volatility, becomes like collyrium,
it should then be known as "coagulated" (saṃmūrchita), even though it may occasionally appear in various colors.
One should raise it up and then cause it to cease within the cavity of the vessel;
thereafter, one should cause that mercury (sūta) to coagulate and thus destroy its sheaths (kañcukīs). Radhy 1.48.
In this manner, one should cause it to coagulate seven times in succession;

Having combined all these together and kneaded them with the juice of *nimbuka*, one should prepare a paste that is smooth like a grindstone.

Of that liquid, there should be as much mercury as constitutes one-fourth part; copper powder should be one-thirty-second part, and salt [one-thirty-second part].

There is no fault in excess, but there is a fault in deficiency.

START *Rasārṇava* 1.52–55 (*pātanasaṃskāra*):
Having removed it from the neck of the cauldron, one should place it inside a cloth pouch.
One should smear the edges of the garments with clay, as if they were stained with mud.
One should place the large pot quickly into the mouth of a water-filled basin;
likewise, one should smear the neck and the joint of the pot with cloth and clay.
One should burn the charcoal from the cauldron for half a watch (yāma) in such a way that the mercury enters the water while the copper remains in the crucible.
This process of dropping the mercury (*rasapātana*) should be performed seven times for it to become pure;
in this manner, subtle defects are dissolved through the repeated cycles of fainting, rising, and falling.

In a cauldron resembling half the size of a jar, a coil of clay is fashioned at the bottom; this is called the "cauldron-binding" (kaṭāhabandha).
Then, having placed that previously prepared pedestal there upon the neck of the cauldron, and having struck a bundle of strong, smooth cloth over it for the sake of covering,
one should smear the edges of that cloth all around with smooth clay so that they become as if fused together.

Then, having placed that cauldron inverted over the mouth of a pot half-filled with water, and having applied a firm seal of cloth and clay at the junction where the rim of the pot meets the base of the cauldron, cow-dung fuel is ignited inside the cauldron for a period of four *ghaṭikās*.
Then, by the heat of the fire, the mercury, having escaped through the pores of the cloth fibers, enters into the water situated within the vessel below.
Furthermore, copper remains adhered only to the wise man.

Then, once again as before, having prepared a crucible of copper filings and mercury, the mercury is precipitated into water using the *kaṭāha-budhna-sajala-sthālī* apparatus, just as previously described.
Thus, when the process of pouring the liquid has been performed seven times, subtle defects such as dullness and inertness depart.
Thus ends the fifth process, the reduction (*pātana*), for the mercury that has been revived from its state of swoon.
START Radhya 1.56–69 (The Rite of Arousing):

In this manner, one should cause the mercury and the mica— both together— to fall [into the crucible] seven times by means of the *pātana* apparatus, rubbing them thoroughly with *kāñjika* juice.
That prepared pill should also be placed in the middle of the bottom of a cooking pot,
together with equal parts of the three myrobalans (triphalā), black mustard (rājikā), fire (vahnī), poison (viṣa), and śigru.
Having thoroughly smeared the upper vessel, one should fashion an excellent casket;
having encased the joint with clay, the *ḍamaru* is the supreme instrument. (Radhy 1.59)

Having abandoned the lower vessel, one should proceed to the upper vessel. (This is the rite of elevation according to another school.)
Kāsīsa, rock salt, and mercury—each equal in measure—to be held for the duration of a day;
indeed, in the absence of kāsīsa, phullatūrikā should be used instead.
One should add them little by little into the mortar and grind the three together;
each [ingredient] should be exactly one hundred niṣkas, neither less nor more at any time.
One should cook it for a day with a fierce fire using the *sthālīsampuṭa* apparatus;
once it has adhered to the upper part and is purified, one should extract that auspicious mercury.
(Thought on the process of raising [the mercury]: 3.

Having made light leaves of copper into a paste with three times as much liquid in a vessel, the mercury is separated from the copper and the copper from the mercury for the purpose of purification (*pātana*).
Having likewise thoroughly ground the two together, one should prepare the paste as before.
One should then place that crucible made of copper and iron into another pot;
the other pot should be turned upside down, and its mouth should be smeared with cloth-clay (vastramṛd).
That which is called the *ḍamaruka* yantra, as well as the one named *vidyādhara*,
should have cow dung placed upon the junction of the vessel's rim.
One should cook the mercury below the lower vessel and above the *bundha* with a mild fire;
the mercury rises into the upper vessel, while the copper remains right there.

This process of raising the mercury is said to be performed seven times; the mercury, having been cast down and then raised, becomes pervasive and clear. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* This work is called "sūtotthāpana" (the raising of mercury). When the mercury has been cast down and subsequently raised, it becomes all-pervasive and pure.
In the preceding yoga, for the purpose of purifying by precipitation (*pātana*), copper was separated from mercury and mercury from copper, each being processed separately for seven cycles.

In this yoga as well, that very same [method] will be employed; however, the distinction is that whereas there it was for the purpose of causing a fall, here it is for the purpose of raising up one who has already fallen.
And that is as follows: RadhyT_1.56–69:3.
Take 66 palas of mercury, 16 palas of copper powder, and 2 palas of salt; having ground all these together in the juice of *nimbuka* fruits, prepare a *pīṭhī* (a thick paste) as before.
Place this in a pot, set another pot over it with its opening facing down, and once the two openings are joined, seal the junction with a cloth and clay.
This is called the *yantra* named *ḍamaruka* and also the *vidyādhara*.
Then, having applied cow dung to the outer side of the base of the upper vessel, one should kindle a mild fire for about one watch (yāma) beneath the base of the lower vessel.
Then the Sūtra, having flown up, goes into the upper vessel.
And the copper remains at the bottom of the vessel.
Furthermore, when the raising of the mercury has been performed in this manner seven times, the mercury becomes pervasive.
That which is called pervasive (vyāpaka) is sharp and has the nature of spreading.
Thus ends the sixth [chapter], the refinement for raising up mercury that has been cast down.
START *Radhy* 1.70–76 (Svedana):
One should form a paste of the leaves of the *śigru* tree with water.
The mass becomes exceedingly soft; one should then form a *kulhaḍī* (small ball) from the mass. Radhy 1.70.
Having discarded the copper, one should throw the entire amount of the risen mercury— thirty-two parts in weight—
into the middle of the previously prepared *prākulhaḍī*.
One should pour *āranāla* and juice derived from *nimbuka* into the vessel;
one should tie a piece of wood around the neck [of the jar] with a cloth previously prepared as a *kulhaḍī*.
One should tie the cloth to a piece of wood so that it does not touch the sour gruel;
likewise, when the pot is covered, one should kindle a mild fire beneath it.
Indeed, for seven days, this should be performed every day for eight watches;
and every day, a fresh *kulhaḍikā* [preparation] should be made with *śigru* leaves. (Radhy 1.74)
Whenever the *cāranāla* is lost, one should repeatedly add fresh material;
the procedure for the sweating (*svedana*) of the mercury should be performed using a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus).

Through the sudorifics, fire has arisen and the rasa has become hungry; now, with its rasa flowing upwards excessively, it endures the fire during digestion. *Rasādhyāyaṭīkā*: Fire has been produced by means of sudorifics, and the *rasa* has become hungry; at present, the *rasa* moving upwards excessively withstands the fire for the purpose of digestion.
Having thoroughly crushed the leaves of the tree named *śigru* until they resemble a paste, one should form a small vessel (*kulhaḍī*) from that mass; into this vessel,
having poured copper according to the previously mentioned method,
one should add the distilled juice as well as salt in the thirty-second part, bind the vessel with a cloth, and [tie] that cloth to a wooden stick with a cord.

Having tied that wood to the neck of the pot with a certain cloth-band, and having poured into the middle of the pot sour gruel (*kāñjika*) mixed with one-third its volume of *nimbu* juice, one should tie a cloth over the sour gruel and attach a *kulhaḍī* (a small strainer) in such a way that the sour gruel does not touch it, but only the steam touches it.
Then, for a day and night, a fire must be kept burning beneath the cooking pot.
Then, having again prepared a fresh *kulhaḍī* with *śigru* leaves, the mercury should be subjected to *sveda* (gentle heating) for a day and night using the *dolāyantra* in the same manner.
And if the previously prepared sour gruel dries up, then fresh sour gruel should be added again.
Thus, having been sweated seven times over seven days with seven *kulhaḍī* vessels, the mercury, when subsequently heated, now withstands an exceedingly intense fire.
Thus ends the seventh refinement, the sweating (*svedana*) of the extracted juice.

With black mustard, salt, radish-root, and asafoetida, each taken in a one-sixteenth part [of the mercury], [one should perform sudation].

The *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) is that by which the substance to be sweated is heated over a fire in a hearth, suspended within a cloth pouch inside a vessel containing sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and medicinal leaves. (Radhy 1.78)
Having folded the cloth into four layers and then enclosed it within a crucible,

Having kindled a fire, one should wash that which is to be taken up with sour gruel;
this is indeed known as the eighth refinement, called "the regulator" (niyāmaka).
Upon the depletion of the *caṇaka* alkali, there should be powder made from *navasāra*;
upon its depletion, that of *sājīkṣāra*, and then the alkali of *jhījaraṭa*.
For its destruction, one should add asafoetida, *pūṣā*, and castor seeds;

This mercury (pārada) has been born exceedingly capable of enduring fire; it is the controller [of the tongue]. For the sake of food, the fickle tongue is always prepared [by it] without hesitation. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* The term *niyāmakaḥ* means that which restrains the tongue from eating unwholesome food. *Saṃskṛtaḥ* means purified by the power of the elixir (*rasāyana*). *Lolā* refers to the tongue, which is naturally restless and fond of various flavors. *Anārtham* means for the purpose of consuming food. *Niḥśaṅkam* means without fear. Thus, the meaning is that this mercury, having been rendered extremely heat-resistant through processing, acts as a constant purifier and regulator of the tongue, enabling one to consume food with confidence.
In the northern direction, there arises a large, red lump of rock-salt from Sindh.

Then, to cover that hole, a pellet of red rock salt (*raktasaindhava*) of the same size should be placed on top.
And in this regard, the following is the understanding:

Then, having dug a pit in the ground the size of an elephant and placed a sealed packet of rock salt (*saindhava*) therein, one should cover it with eight *aṅgula*s of dust, fill the pit with powdered dried cow-dung (*chagaṇa*), and ignite a fire. Then, in the morning, having extracted [the substance] and washed it with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should place it again in a salt packet, pour resin powder (*navasāra*) and lime juice over it, close the packet, place it back in the pit, and maintain a fire of dried cow-dung (*kārīṣa*) for a day and night.

Likewise, when one has a slight desire to eat, one moves the tongue.

A vessel filled with sour gruel and saturated with the juice of *nimbuka* fruits, containing a *bījapūraka* fruit submerged within it by means of a *dolāyantra* (swing-apparatus). Radhy 1.108.
Having bound and sealed [the vessel], one should ignite a fierce fire beneath it for seven days; every day, the mouth [of the vessel] should be opened with fresh *mātuliṅga* fruits. 1.109.
When its mouth is opened by means of mercury (*sūta*), it swallows substances such as mica (*abhraka*);
with its mouth wide open, it indeed swallows everything that is thrown in and digests it all.

Having uprooted the stalk of a fully ripe *bījapūra* fruit, having carved out its interior and made a cavity,
one should then pour in the obstructing liquid (*nirodhaka-rasa*), place salt on top, cover it again with that same stalk, tie the *bījapūraka* in a cloth,
and [place it] in the middle of a vessel filled with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) mixed with one-third lemon juice, using the aforementioned *dolāyantra*.
Having placed a citron fruit submerged in sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should maintain a fire burning beneath it for a day and night.

Thus, having been processed with nine new *mātuluṅga* fruits seven times over seven days, the essence has its mouth opened wide for the swallowing of *dhānyābhraka* and other minerals; it digests every morsel given to it according to the prescribed method.

Then, having broken that pot and taken the liquid, one should again place mercury, grain-sulphur, mica, salt, and the juice of *nimbu* into a second small pot; as before, by means of intense heating for a day and night, a *pala* of grain-sulphur and mica is to be digested.
In this manner, over eight days, using eight small jars, one should digest eight *pala* measures of each of the eight types of mineral ores and mica.

And with the water of *agasti* flowers, the juice of white lotuses,
*varṣābhū*, *taṇḍulīya*, black pepper, and *sumukha*.

One should heat the mercury, bound with a paste of long pepper (*marica*), *asurī*, white mustard (*siddhārtha*), and poison,

When the juice has been thus steamed, the wise man should then crush the *yavaciñcī* plant, including its roots and leaves, and mix it with *kāñjika*.
O Goddess, in the *kāñjika* [fermented gruel] there is always produced a binding of essence;
in the process of gold-making, the "gold-mouthed" is applied to gold, and the "silver-mouthed" is applied to silver.

The characteristic of the "decayed" [poison] should be known as that of a water-creature (jalaukā) holding a staff;

In this manner, the wise one should digest the mercury that has been processed with the six qualities.
That which adheres quickly to the ground when thrown is called *dhānyābhra* (grain-iron).

First, having filled a cloth pouch with mica, unbroken grains of rice, and fine pebbles and gravel, and having fastened the opening securely with a cord, one should place it inside a wooden vessel filled with water and rub it vigorously so that the mica is ground into powder and some of it escapes slightly to the outside.

When the sixfold processed *dhānyābhra* has been digested, it does not fly out externally.

Thus, when the mouth is extended, the first [stage] is the "digestion" (*jāraṇa*) consisting of the swallowing of the sky by the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

That iron mortar in which four feet are supported by a small stool is called "four-footed" (catuṣpāda).

In that iron mortar, having added mercury in which mica has been consumed, as well as sixty-four parts of iron filings relative to the mercury, one should grind it very gently with *viḍa* salt and a lump of clay.

For this purpose, the mercury, having been bound by means of an infusion of iron powder, becomes the color of wheat.
Likewise, he endures passions.

START *Rādhya* 1.156–161 (*bhūdharayantra*, definition):
A pit filled with earth, smeared with lime or with powdered brick mixed with molasses.
When it is thoroughly smeared with clay and has dried, this machine is considered a "earth-bearer" (bhūdhara).
Having placed mercury along with the streak known as "worn gold" (*jīrṇahema*) into a *bhūdhara* furnace, one should add pure powdered sulfur in a sixteenth part [of the mercury]. (Radhy 1.157)
One should place a small pot with its opening facing downwards inside the lid;
one should then coat it with cloth and clay and ignite a fierce fire. (Radhy 1.158)
One should repeatedly add a sixteenth part [of mercury], and likewise a small amount (koḍīyaka) repeatedly,
until the pure sulphur is digested, having become six times the weight of the mercury.
There shall be firmness through passion when mercury has digested the sulphur;
likewise silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, and brass [are transformed]. (Radhy 1.160)

One should melt bell-metal and the seven metals after anointing them with *rasa*; thus they will indeed take on the color of the lunar day (*tithi*), becoming gold—of this there is no doubt. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* Bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) consists of copper and zinc. The "seven metals" are iron, copper, tin, lead, brass, silver, and gold. One should first grind these seven metals together with mercury (*rasa*) until they become a paste, then apply it to the bell-metal and melt it. By this process, the metal takes on the color corresponding to the lunar day; there is no doubt that it becomes gold. The term "lunar day" (*tithi*) refers to the number of the lunar day from one to fifteen. For example, if one applies the mixture on the first lunar day, the metal becomes white like silver; if on the second, it becomes yellow like gold; if on the third, it becomes red like copper; and so forth. Thus, by applying the mercury-paste according to the specific lunar day, one obtains gold of various colors. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "becomes gold" implies that even if the resulting color is not the pure yellow of gold, it becomes a substance resembling gold, such as a reddish-yellow or whitish-yellow hue. Therefore, one should apply the mercury-paste on the lunar day corresponding to the specific color one desires to achieve. This is the intent of the verse. The mention of "bell-metal" is illustrative; it means that one should apply the mercury-paste to any of the base metals, such as iron or copper, and then melt them. The "seven metals" are those mentioned above. One should grind these seven metals with mercury, apply the paste to the chosen base metal, and then melt it. By this method, the metal attains the color of the lunar day and becomes gold. There is no doubt about this. The commentary on the *Rasādhyāya*. 1.161.

In this case, a pit measuring one *hasta* in length and breadth is bound with bricks like a well; it is smeared within with lime mixed with cow-dung, or alternatively, with a powder mixed with molasses. Once dried, this machine is called the *bhūdhara* (earth-supporter).

Then, having placed mercury (sūta) with a sixteenth part of pure sulphur powder— or alternatively, a brass vessel coated with clay and a broken earthenware bowl with a golden rim— inside [the crucible], and having applied a lid of clay coated with glass (kāca) over it, and having smeared it with cloth-and-clay (karpaṭamṛttikā),
one should place that sealed pair of bowls into the middle of a *bhūdhara* furnace and ignite it with a fierce fire (*haṭhāgni*).
And the pure nature of sulphur is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.
For, throughout this entire treatise and elsewhere as well, pure sulphur alone is the seed for the two roots of *kīcana*.
Therefore, it should be understood that this method for purifying sulfur is kept secret in all [tantras].
If sulphur is processed while still containing impurities, the desired result will not be achieved; therefore, the purification of sulphur must be understood from the mouth of the Guru.

Likewise, when sixteen parts of the previously added sulphur have been digested, one should again add sixteen parts of sulphur along with the fumes of *koḍīyaka* and *mūrchā*, and having applied *koḍīyaka*, the fire should be ignited forcefully.
In this way, when six times the amount of pure sulphur has been digested by the mercury, the mercury becomes exceedingly red.

By smearing that juice upon the seven metals—silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, brass, and bell-metal—and melting them, they become fifteen-fold gold. Thus ends the fifth [section], the digestion of sulfur by one who has mastered the *hemarāji* elixir.

*dāghī*, *chedaka*, *kaṣā*, *āvarta*, and *śodhana*; by these, gold is purified.

In this case, there is chalk.
Salt.
The fourth.
Just as experts examine gold by means of these five types of clay—namely, red ochre, *jīkaka*, and so forth—in that same manner [should one examine the mind].

Having moistened gold leaves with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should powder them together with an equal portion of salt—along with the dry *tūri* (camphor) and *lagada* (a medicinal resin) discarded by a washerman—and place them in a crucible (*karpara*).

Then, layering the leaves and the powder alternately—leaf, then powder, then leaf again, and so on, placing leaves one above the other—one should finally place another crucible on top and cover all sides completely with the powder. As many [layers as required]...
The earthenware vessel is covered; having broken up as many dried cow-dung cakes as are required and applied fire, it is released [from the heat] if it remains burning by itself.
Then, once again, on the second occasion, a sealed packet (puṭa) filled with pieces of dried cow-dung (chagaṇaka) should be applied.
Thus, if there is an excess of impurity (*mala*), then the third [remedy] should be applied.
In this same way, the same effect is achieved by using colored chalk, or even white chalk mixed with salt, by applying it two or three times over the two layers.
Now, if it is understood in this way:
Even when this has been done, if the substance is not entirely pure because of an excess of base metals such as copper and the like,
then, by means of a coating of *āmrasāra* (mango-stone) or *jīraka* (cumin) mixed with salt, according to the previous method, all impurities are purified by applying two or three layers (*puṭas*).
Thus, by means of the five types of clay, there is purification from all defects.

Likewise, in the present time, fourteen *vaṇikas*, ten *daśīkas*, eleven *yanas*, and nine *vās* constitute the ultimate limit for gold; beyond this, even if purification is performed, there is no increase in the *karṇikā*.
Furthermore, if the refining powder is blown [into the crucible], then whatever metal such as silver has been consumed is also recovered.
Likewise, having placed silver in a crucible, lead is thrown on top and heated from below; then both, becoming fused together in a single mass, circulate.
Thereupon, the lead and silver dross, having flowed through, meets in the middle of the crucible at a point measuring a finger-breadth in width, adhering to the interior wall of the crucible.
And if the pure silver essence remains even when one is deluded, then it should be known as the pure silver essence.
When protection has been meditated upon and the clay has been processed, the relics are obtained.

Having placed digested sulphur and mercury into an earthenware crucible (śarāvasampuṭa) within an earth-supporting apparatus (bhūdharayantra), and having added the essence of realgar (manaḥśilāsattva) in a thirty-second part,
one should apply a seal (koḍīyaka) to the opening, coat it with cloth and clay, and ignite a fierce fire. Once the essence of realgar has been digested,
one should again add a thirty-second part of that [mercury].
In this manner, the essence of realgar, which is like a thread for repeated casting, should be processed.
Neither deficient nor excessive.
In this way, when the *manaḥśilā* spirit has been digested by mercury, the seven metals, having been melted after being anointed [with it], become forms of gold.
And that gold endures purification by means of the five types of earth.
In that way, it becomes purified by the removal of the impurities of the whirlpools of grasping.
Thus ends the sixth [section]: the digestion of the essence of realgar by mercury that has been processed with sulphur.
A mercury processed with this many refinements is indeed a true alchemical agent for metal.
Furthermore, those processes which follow from this, as well as the various digestions (*jāraṇā*), are the means for accomplishing the body and [alchemical] metals.
In this regard, he explains the seventh [topic], the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of base metals (*khāpara*) and living beings (*sattva*).

Then, having filtered that powder, one should cast it into all types of metal; while they are being strained, it will permeate a thousand [parts], acting as a penetrator (*pravedhaka*). *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* Having strained that powder, one should place it into all metals such as gold and the like. While those metals are being strained, this [powder] will permeate a thousand [times its own weight]. It is called a "penetrator" because it enters into the interior of the metal. It is said that even if the metal is not strained, the essence of the powder will enter into it. Alternatively, it may mean that the powder should be placed into the metal after it has been strained. *Pravedha* means entry or penetration. It is called a "thousand-penetrator" because it enters into a thousand parts [of the metal]. It is said that by means of this, the metal becomes as soft as wax. This is the meaning. *Rasādhyāya*, verse 218.

In this case, first, having made a leaf from a single leaf of pure nāga by cutting it into one part, and having poured into it mercury measured at the size of a *rati*, one should melt the thin [mercury] situated on the leaf of *nārā* and, having prepared a crucible (*veḍhanī*), one should melt that [mercury] in the crucible.
Thereupon, it becomes powder.

Then, having melted all the previously mentioned metals such as nāga and vaṅga in quantities of one thousand *rati*s each, while the liquid metal is still swirling, one should throw into it a powder of *veḍhanī* juice in the measure of one *rati*.
Then, the gold adhering to the bottom should be collected.
This is the mercury that pierces through a thousand [times].
Thus ends the seventeenth [chapter], the purification by transmutation (*vedhakasaṃskāra*) of the mercury that has been made to step forward.
START *Rasārṇava* 1.219–223 (Opening):
When one *gadyāṇa* of lead has been melted, one should cast in a *gadyāṇa* of mercury.
And one *gadyāṇa* of sulfur should be thrown into the midst of that powder.
When four *gadyāṇas* of *sarjikā* have been added together, the powder should be ground finely and then stirred with water. (Radhy 1.220)
Having placed [the object] inside a pair of earthenware bowls,
one should dig a pit measuring one cubit in size, fill it with dry cow-dung, and cover it with a layer of clay and airtight cloth.
Having placed the pair of earthen bowls into a pit, one should then kindle a fire;
once it has become cool to the touch, one should take that [substance] and reduce it to a fine powder. Radhy 1.222.

Then, when the pierced mercury has been melted, having thrown [the powder] into it in the measure of a mustard seed, if this is done, the opening of the mercury certainly occurs. (Radhy 1.223) *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* When the pierced mercury has been liquefied, one should cast [the medicinal powder] into it in the quantity of a mustard seed. By doing so, the breaking open of the mercury is assured.
Then, in the midst of that powder, there is one *gadyāṇaka* of sulfur.
And one *gadyāṇaka* shall be added for each *sarjikā*.

Then, having combined four *gadyāṇakas*— one of purified lead (*nāga*), two of mercury (*sūta*), and one of sulphur (*gandhaka*)— and having ground them thoroughly into a powder, stirred it with water, dried it again, and placed it inside a pair of earthen saucers (*śarāva-sampuṭa*),
one should apply cloth-and-clay (*vastra-mṛttikā*) to the joint of the saucers and then [bury it] in the middle of a pit measuring one cubit in depth.

Having placed cow-dung cakes on top and applied a pair of earthen saucers as a lid, one should release it; then, having broken it into pieces with cow-dung cakes on the sides and above, the fire should be ignited.
And if, after burning, it does not remain by itself, then one should take the medicinal substance from the middle of the crucible, reduce it to a fine powder,
and throw that fine powder— measuring a mustard seed or four *gadyāṇas*— into the middle of the strained mercury that has been processed by *vedha*.
And here, within the context of the elixir (sūta), the dosage of the medicinal substance to be added has been stated.
But not so for one whose essence has been pierced.
Likewise, his teachers have not stated that this [scripture] is authoritative.
Therefore, it is known by means of inference.
Afterwards, sixty-four palas of liquid are prescribed for all [the preparations].

Then, with that much mercury— just as much as is required when the medicinal processing (*auṣadhavedhasaṃskāra*) is being performed— one should cast four *gadyāṇaka* full of the medicinal juice, measuring only a mustard seed, into the middle of it.
By day, by the command of the venerable Guru, he knows it to whatever extent it may be.
In this way, when powder the size of a mustard seed is thrown [into it], the opening of the pierced mercury occurs.
That which is called "unsealing" (udghāṭana) pertains to the piercing of all elements and the removal of all diseases.
Thus ends the eighteenth consecration.
START Radhy 1.224–230 (Gold: *rāji*):
One part of the "living" copper (*jīvaśulva*) and two parts of pure gold [are to be used].
One should fashion three equal segments with rounded edges and well-formed joints.
Having swallowed a snake killed with realgar using the juices of *nimbuka* fruits,
one should apply a plaster of that [substance] to both wings of the "stiff-winged" [bird].
Having ground together one-sixth part of *cittrakūṭa* and one-sixth part of salt,
a cooking pot (*sthālikā*) should then be filled with equal portions of these.
One should place a smeared leaf in the middle of that, submerged and rising upward;
when an inverted earthen bowl is placed over it, one should seal the rim tightly with clay.
Then, one should place an inverted *ḍhaṅkaṇī* (a small vessel) upon a shallow bowl;
beneath the cooking pot, one should forcefully kindle a fire for four watches (twelve hours). Radhy 1.228.
Indeed, by that very procedure, there shall be three incisions on the leaf;
having taken the middle incision, one should discard the two side incisions. (Radhy 1.229)

By means of the powder of *madhyaphāḍī*, a line of gold will certainly be produced; by adding sixty-four parts [of this], the mercury is to be digested, becoming eight times its original weight. (Radhy 1.230) *Commentary: Rasādhyāyaṭīkā:* By means of the powder of *madhyaphāḍī*, a streak of gold will certainly appear. By adding sixty-four parts [of this powder], the mercury is to be processed until it increases eightfold in weight from the original mercury.
In this context, having killed the mercury by means of *māna* and *śulba*, it is brought back to life; they call that living mercury *jīvanta*.
Then, having melted together one part of that copper and two parts of gold—thus three parts in total—one should fashion that into a thick leaf.
Then, having killed the lead with realgar and the juice of *nimbuka* fruits, the leaf of lac should be smeared on both sides with that killed lead.

Then, having made a powder by equal parts of red chalk (citrakūṭakhaṭī) and salt, fill a pot with it; place a leaf floating upright in its center, set an earthen saucer upside down over its mouth, smear the rim with clay, and place a lid (ḍhaṅkaṇī) inverted over the saucer; then [heat] for four watches (prahara) beneath the pot.
The fire of *haṭha* should be kindled.
When this is done, three incisions are produced in the leaf.
Then, taking that which is the middle strip and discarding the two side strips to be ground, the powder of the middle strip is called the "golden streak" (*hemarājī*).
A sixty-fourth part of that should be added to the previously mentioned mercury according to the method stated before.
In this manner, up until eight times [the amount], having added a gold streak, it becomes liquefied according to the previously stated method.
Thus ends the *Sarvotkṛṣṭā Hemarājī*.
START *Radhy* 1.231–235 (lead:: *rāji*):
Lead-line (*nāgarāji*) is considered common; gold-line (*mākṣikī*) is recorded as middling.
And the supreme Ghoṣarāji is that which is superior to the Prakāśā. Radhy 1.231.
One *pala* of sharp iron, two *palas* of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), nine *palas* of copper, and three *palas* of brass (*pittala*). (Radhy 1.232)
The wise one should cast thirty *pala* of the stone of a dead serpent, along with [an amount of] *tithi*-numbered *pala*, into a crucible and cause it to be melted.
Then, having added seven and a half *palas* of gold-mercury (*suvarṇamākṣika*) little by little, the wise one should cause it to boil slowly.
When the portion of copper becomes equal to that [of the other metal],
there shall be a slight streak of luster; this is proclaimed as the first [stage].
In this context, that which is a common serpent-lineage is one that performs only minor tasks.
The row of bees performs the function of the middle way.
The line of *vyoṣa* (the three pungents) is excellent and performs many functions.
The iron-like bright streak (*ayaḥprakāśarāji*) is the best among all those streaks; the meaning is that it is the most excellent of all.
Then, first, the row of iron-light is described.
One pala of brass and two palas of bell-metal.
Nine *pala* of pure copper and three *pala* of bell-metal (*pittalā*).
Fifteen palas of realgar that has been processed with mercury.
In this manner, thirty palas of all the counted [substances] should be cast into the crucible and melted.

Then, having brought seven and a half palas of gold-mercury (suvarṇamākṣika) and having thrown a small amount into the middle, one should again slowly rotate it until it becomes equal in measure to the portion of copper.
This is the meaning. RadhyT 1.231–235:11.
There are nine copper *palas*.
Then, when all the liquid has been stirred and it reaches the measure of nine palas, that first streak which appears like iron is called *ayaḥprakāśarāji*.
Thus is described the row of light of the supreme iron [element].
START Radhy 1.236–237 (bronze:: rāji):
An equal amount of bronze powder [is to be added] to the powder of sharp iron.
Having thrown it in and stirred it within the crucible, it is made into a single mass.

Having added lead (nāga) equal to half the weight of the *piṇḍa*, one should repeatedly subject it to digestion (*jārya*). When the lead has been digested, there will be a row of sounds (*ghoṣarāji*); and when [the lead] is digested, [it occurs] with six times the amount of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*). *Rasādhyāyaṭīkā*: One should add lead equal to half the weight of the *piṇḍa* and digest it again and again. Once the lead is digested, there arises a "row of sounds" (*ghoṣarāji*); and when [the lead] is digested, [it occurs] with six times the amount of bell-metal.
Having placed equal quantities of powdered steel and powdered bell-metal into a crucible, one then melts them together and forms them into a single mass.
Then, having placed half a mātrā of pure nāga from that *piṇḍa* into the middle of the crucible (*mūṣā*), it should be repeatedly rotated and subjected to *jāraṇā*.
Then again, having cast the *nāga* with half a measure, it should be brought to maturity.
Furthermore, if this process of digestion is repeated again and again, six times the amount of lead (*nāga*) becomes digested within the bell-metal (*kāṃsya*).
Then a streak of *vyoṣa* arises.
Thus, "vyoṣarāji" means a streak of bronze.
START *Rādhya* 1.238–239 (*mākṣika*:: *rāji*):
One should melt separately four *pala*s of pure copper.
Four palas of thūthāpalāni and four palas of honey.
One should add the powder of Palāśa leaves little by little until only copper remains; this is considered the *mākṣīkaja* (derived from honey) *rāji*.
*Rasādhyāyaṭīkā* Commentary: One should add the powder of Palāśa leaves little by little until only copper remains; this is considered the *mākṣīkaja* (derived from honey) *rāji*.

First, having separately melted four *pala* of pure copper, one should then add to its midst four *pala* of *thūthā* (antimony) and eight *pala* of *mākṣika* (pyrite) reduced to powder; adding these little by little and repeatedly stirring, one should cause it to digest until [the desired state] is reached.
Until only the copper remains.
The meaning is that four *palas* of every medicinal herb are to be digested [in the fire].
Thus ends the third [chapter], the *Mākṣikarāji*.
START Radhy 1.240–242:
One should slowly and separately process one part of mercury (śulva) with eight parts of killed lead (mṛtanāga) and four parts of thūthā using a stone [mortar]. (Radhy 1.240)
Having ground it into powder, one should add it little by little to the molten metal (*śulba*); this will become a row of *nāga*s. (Radhy 1.241)
Having melted one part of pure copper in a crucible, then add four parts of realgar, four parts of killed lead, and likewise four parts of thuthaka.
Having thus reduced the twelve parts to powder and added a small amount into the middle of the molten copper, one should cause it to be stirred until only the copper remains.
This is called the "Nāgarājī" (Queen of Serpents) meter.

Regarding the fruit of the *thūthā* (mercury) royal lines, he says "of the elevated metals of the kingdom" and so forth; having made a powder of the metal for each of the four royal lines, one should apply each line individually.
Within the liquid, according to the previously mentioned method for liquids, eight times the amount should be digested in sequence; this is the procedure for making it royal (*rājikaraṇa*).
Thus ends the fourth [chapter], the King of Nagas.
START *Rasārṇava* 1.243–249 (Extraction of the Essence of Khāpara):
Now follows the procedure for the extraction of the essence of khāpara.
Then, having boiled one *maṇa* of mercury with human urine for three days and dried it in the sun, one should cook it for one watch (*yāma*) with milk. (Radhy 1.243)
When it has dried, one-eighth part of powdered *khala* should be added to it, along with a fourth part of *ṭaṅkaṇa* alkali and one-eighth part of the previously mentioned jaggery. (Radhy 1.244)
When two crucibles made of clay have been prepared, round in shape like a *kacūla*,
one should place a crucible filled with powder inside the other.

Furthermore, on the western side, one should place a clay vessel with its opening at the top and its base at the bottom, fourteen finger-breadths in height, and having a hole at its base. One should set that [nozzle] facing downwards.
And one should strike the entire [surface] all around with clay mixed with cow-dung;
indeed, a device made of gourds and reeds must be employed for the precipitation of the essence.

One should place the apparatus inside the furnace and repeatedly blow into it until it is completely filled with the charcoal of dead wood from *babbūla*, *khadira*, and other such trees. (Radhy 1.248)
And with similar [materials], one should support the *mukhī* [crucible] from within a *tumbī* or *nalī*;
everything up to the surrounding casing (*veṣāparīyaka*) should be held from within the crucible (*mūṣā*).
— *Rasādhyāyaṭīkā* (Commentary) on verse 1.249.

Having boiled one *maṇa* of *rasaka* (borax) with human urine for three days, dried it in the sun, cooked it for one *prahara* with milk, and dried it again, one should powder it and add to it these three: *khala* (impurity/salt) in an eighth part, *ṭaṅkaṇa-kṣāra* (borax) in a fourth part, and the aforementioned jaggery in an eighth part.

Then, having fashioned two crucibles out of clay, robust and circular in shape like small bowls, one should place the previously mentioned powder of khāpara into one crucible and suspend that crucible upside down over the tube.

Then, having made all sides seamless with rags and clay, such a machine called a *tumbanalī* should be constructed for the precipitation of the essence (*sattva*). Then, having filled the interior of the crucible (*koṭhī*) with the drosses (*līhālaka*) of *babbūla*, *khadira*, *āmalī*, and so forth, and having placed the machine therein, one should blow [the bellows] repeatedly and, using tongs, [turn] the tube of the machine downward.
Having been shaken, whatever amount of essence flows down from the middle and enters the lower crucible—that is called the *khāpara-sattva*.
Thus ends the procedure for the precipitation of copper-sattva.
START *Rasārṇava* 1.250–253 (The Extraction of the Essence of Realgar):
Now follows the procedure for extracting the essence (*sattva*) of realgar (*manaḥśilā*).
The wise should grind the best realgar with mercury in a mortar;
having placed it in a glass flask, one should seal its opening with mica.
One should place powdered burnt stone mixed with salt upon the head [of the vessel],
and one should smear the entire water-pot with cloth and clay.
Having broken a baked jar and placed a clay-coated pot upon its neck,
the fire of *haṭha* should be ignited below for twelve *yāmas*, O Maṇi.
The interior of the crucible shall become empty, and the essence drips into the neck [of the vessel].

Having broken the crucible, the wise person should diligently extract the essence from the stone. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* The interior of the crucible becomes void; the essence flows into the neck of the vessel. After breaking the crucible, the intelligent practitioner should carefully take up the essence from the stone.
Having ground the finest *kaṇayarī* and realgar (*manaḥśilā*) in a mortar, one should place them in a crucible (*kumpa*), seal the mouth of the crucible with mica (*abhraka*),
and apply a mixture of salt and powdered burnt stone upon its top. Having covered the entire crucible with cloth and clay,
a fierce fire must be maintained beneath the realgar for a period of twelve *praharas*.
Then the creature flies up and clings to the throat, and Kumbhodara becomes empty.
In this way, having broken the jar, the being clinging to the neck should be seized.
Thus is the procedure for the precipitation of metallic essences from stones.
Now, the threefold method for liquefying the six metals is as follows:
START Radhya 1.254–263 (Gold::
Alchemy) Even a dead frog may be found anywhere; by means of this [substance], it [is transformed].
Rock crystal and ṭaṅkaṇa alkali; its pills, moreover, should be very fine.
Then, having split open the belly of a frog, those fine pellets should be placed inside;
one should then put that frog into a pot smeared with ghee, oil, and other substances. Radhy 1.255.
Having placed a *pradhvarā* and a *ḍhaṅkaṇī* [on top], the cooking-pot (*sthālī*) is buried in the ground;
then, after sixty days have passed, the pot is drawn up from the earth. (Radhy 1.256)
Having thus purified it from the middle of the vessel, that entire substance should be taken;
having placed it all in a mortar, it should be ground into an extremely fine powder.
Then, having filtered a *gadyāṇa* of snow-born mercury colored with the lunar digits,
the wise should add a *valla* of frog-powder into its midst.
No bondage arises for gold; it is merely produced in a liquid form.
This is indeed what is called the liquefaction of gold, brought about by those who possess knowledge of it. (Radhy 1.259)
Just as there is a golden liquefaction when mercury is placed inside gold,
so too does it occur with magnetite, silver, tin, and lead. (Radhy 1.260)
The powder [of mercury] acts as a sixteen-fold penetrator (vedhaka) into copper and all six metals;
furthermore, when any one of those six metals has been melted, it acts as such.
One should add frog-powder to a single *gadyāṇa* of iron and a small amount of cloth;
that iron will become liquid, and it will flow by its very name.

The liquefaction of the six metals has been performed by those who know it through ritual practice (*sakarmaṇā*). Whatever operations are to be described hereafter regarding these [metals] shall be performed upon the metallic ores (*dhātuṣu*). *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* The liquefaction of the six metals has been accomplished by experts through the application of ritual procedures. Whatever processes are to be explained subsequently concerning these [metals] are to be carried out upon the metallic ores.

Having cut open the belly of a frog that has died naturally, one should place therein extremely fine pellets of crystalline, brilliant *ṭaṅkaṇa* salt; then, having smeared it with ghee, oil, and so forth, one places the frog inside a vessel, covers it with a lid,
and buries the vessel in the ground.
After sixty days, one should again take out the vessel, collect everything from within it, grind it in a mortar, and prepare a powder.
Then, having melted the finest gold *gadyāṇaka*, one should throw into its center frog-powder measuring only a *valla*.
Then that gold does not attain a solid bond again, but remains only in a liquid state.
This indeed becomes the liquefaction of gold.
And when this liquid gold is melted in an amount of one *gadyāṇa* with any of the following—copper, silver, tin, lead, or copper—one *valla* of frog-powder is thrown into it.
Thereupon, all of them become liquid, and each becomes a "liquid" (*druti*) named after its respective metal.
These are the liquefaction of iron, the liquefaction of silver, the liquefaction of tin, the liquefaction of lead, and the liquefaction of copper.
Thus ends the first [section], on the liquefaction of the six metals.
START *Rasārṇava* 1.264–267 (Gold:: Melting): From the very Pītāṅga [mineral], prepare the dālī and the five-fold [preparation] in small pieces.
And having ignited it in an earthen pot, one should reduce it to fine ash.
At the end of the remainder [of the ritual], one should perform the five-limbed rite during the night;
with the juice of that very [plant], an infusion of this ash itself should be administered.
When one *gadyāṇa* has been melted— whether it be of the color of the lunar days (*tithi*) or born of gold—
one should then repeatedly add a *valla* at a time of the ashes.

In this manner, one *gadyāṇaka* is always to be refined within a *gadyāṇa*; thus the liquefaction of gold is achieved—this is the procedure for all metals. *Rasādhyāyaṭīkā*: [Commentary] Thus, within a *gadyāṇa*, one *gadyāṇaka* is always to be purified. In this way, the melting of gold is accomplished; this method applies to all metals.

Having prepared five-part pieces of yellow *devadālī* and roasted them in an earthen pot, they should be thoroughly reduced to ash. Then, an infusion of that very *devadālī* juice must be administered to that ash.
Next, having melted a *gadyāṇaka* of fifteen-variety gold, one should add a dose (*valla*) of the *devadālī* ash and cause it to be assimilated (*jāraṇīya*).
Furthermore, when, by repeatedly throwing in only a *valla* at a time, a *gadyāṇaka*’s worth of ash has been consumed, then the liquefaction of gold (*kāñcanadruti*) occurs.
In the same way, even for iron and other metals, a liquefaction (druti) occurs under their respective names by means of the digestion (jāraṇa) of the ash of *devadālī*.
Thus ends the second [section], on the liquefaction of the six metals.
START *Rasārṇava* 1.268–269 (*Ṣaḍlohadrutikaraṇa* [3]): One should burn white *devadālī* and the five parts of *aṅga* in a crucible.
The impregnation with cow urine should be performed twenty-one times for the ash.

Then, the procedure previously described should be performed for all six metals; thus, liquefaction occurs in the six metals without a doubt. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* Then, the procedure previously described should be performed for all six metals; thus, liquefaction occurs in the six metals without a doubt. "Should be performed" means it must be carried out. "Thus" (*evam*) means by this method. "Liquefaction" (*druti*) means the state of being liquid. "In the six metals" means in iron and the other five. "Without a doubt" (*na saṃśayaḥ*) means there is no uncertainty. This is the sense. Having prepared five parts of the white *devadālī* plant and incinerated them in an earthen pot, one should reduce them to ash; then, having administered twenty-one saturations of that ash with cow urine, the white *devadālī* ash should be smeared onto the six metals as before.
The melting of all metals occurs.
