START *Rasādhyāya* 1.270–271 (The killing of various metals):
Realgar destroys lead (*nāga*), and yellow orpiment destroys tin (*vaṅgaka*).
Likewise, iron with cinnabar, copper, and pure sulfur.

Silver, sesame, honey, and gold are killed by lead; the procedure for copper that has been taught is the same procedure for the killing of these five. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* Silver, sesame, honey, and gold are killed by lead; the procedure for copper that has been taught is the same procedure for the killing of these five.
By means of realgar, lead is killed; by yellow orpiment, tin; by cinnabar, iron; by pure sulphur, copper; by sesame and honey, silver; and by lead, gold is killed.
Then, by whichever method... [is applied].
START *Radhy* 1.272–275 (Copper: *māraṇa*):
Having made either a leaf or a powder of copper, the wise one should release it separately.
And pure sulfur powder, doubled in amount from the copper.
Having ground that [substance] with the juice of *kumārī* or, if that is unavailable, with milk, one should insert a copper leaf inside two cakes (*pūpa*) made from it. Radhy 1.273.
Having placed that inside a pair of earthen bowls, sealed it with clay,
and smeared the joint with cloth and clay, one should place that packet into a cauldron.

Having placed pieces of charcoal into an iron pan, one should then ignite the fire; when it has burned down and become cool, the wise should collect the copper, which is now dead (reduced to ash). *Commentary: Rasādhyāyaṭīkā:* Having cast small pieces of charcoal into an iron pan, one should subsequently kindle the fire. Once the fire has subsided and the pan has cooled, the wise should take up the copper, which has been reduced to a state of death (i.e., converted to calx).

Having made either a leaf or a powder of copper, one should then take double that amount of pure sulfur powder and grind it thoroughly with *kumārī* juice or milk. Having formed two cakes and placed the previously prepared copper leaf or powder in the middle, one should place the two cakes inside a pair of earthen saucers (*śarāva*), seal the joint with cloth and clay, and [place them] on all sides...
Having smeared it with clay and placed it inside a cauldron within a pair of earthen bowls, one should fill the cauldron with chaff and set it on fire.
Then, having been heated until it has cooled, the dead copper should be collected.
Thus ends the procedure for the killing of copper.
By the same procedure by which copper is killed with sulphur here, the five metals beginning with lead (nāga) should likewise be killed when required for the purpose.
Thus ends the procedure for the killing of the six metals.
START *Rasārṇava* 1.276–287:
Now, the threefold digestion of diamond using food and medicinal substances (*annapathyahīrakakaraṇa*), and the fivefold calcination (*pañcadhāmāraṇa*)—
[this is] the digestion of diamond using food and medicinal substances (1).
One should remove the stalk of a citron fruit and make a small hole;
having placed a genuine diamond within it, one should cover it with the stalk. (Radhy 1.276)
One should wrap an entire citron fruit with cloth and clay;
then, one should prepare a pit measuring one cubit in length, depth, and width.
Once that pit has been filled with soil prepared by the followers of Cāṇakya, one should cover its opening with a bowl of *bījapūraka* fruit;
thereafter, one should cast fire into its center.
Once it has been ignited and has become cool, this ritual consisting of nine times should be performed again and again with fresh *bījapūraka* fruits.
Having rolled it into a very fine ball in the evening, one should place it inside that lump;
the ball is then placed within a pair of earthenware bowls.
A previously prepared pit should be filled again with chaff placed by the followers of Cāṇakya;
its surface smeared with cloth and clay, the wise man should cook [the victim] within that pit. (Radhy 1.281)
One should repeatedly cook it nine times with these mare’s urine;
then, there shall be the branch of the royal jujube tree, consisting of tender sprouts. (Radhy 1.282)
Then, having taken that [mold], the wise man should make a hole in its interior;
having placed *nesa* and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) below and above, he should insert that diamond.
Then, with clay from the cloth, one should fill the branches and sprouts so they are dense;
this is done in nine ways according to the previous method in the pit previously dug.
Having made a hole in a pill composed of asafoetida, one should place a diamond inside, cover its opening with asafoetida, and then place it upon a pedestal of black gram flour. Radhy 1.285.
Having cast it into a vessel filled with that oil, one should ignite a fire beneath it;
in this manner, using the appropriate technique, the process should be performed nine times for each fresh piece of asafoetida.

By this method, a high-quality diamond of the three paths (*tripatha*) clearly arises. Having ground it with *thūthāviḍa*, the wise one causes it to be digested in the liquid (*rasa*). *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* By this method, a high-quality diamond of the three paths clearly arises. Having ground it with *thūthāviḍa*, the wise one causes it to be digested in the liquid (*rasa*).
Having uprooted the stalk of a citron fruit and carved out its center to create a cavity, one should place a genuine diamond within it and cover the top with the stalk.

Then, having wrapped the entire citron fruit in clay mixed with cloth, one should dig a pit one cubit deep, one cubit wide, and one cubit long at the bottom; having filled it with dried cow-dung cakes that have been placed therein, [one should set the fruit inside].
In that regard, having removed the citron fruit and placed a clay bowl over its opening, fire should be applied to the cow-dung cakes.

Then, once it has burned and cooled down, one should first take another citron fruit and perform everything as before; having thrown the diamond into the pit along with the citron fruit and ignited the cow-dung cakes, when they have cooled, the diamond should be taken from the middle of the citron fruit.

In this manner, that very diamond should be cooked nine times with fresh *bījapūra* fruits. Then, having rolled it in *vaḍavāikāni* and formed it into a ball, that same diamond should be placed in the center of it.

Next, having placed that ball inside a pair of earthen saucers (*śarāvasampuṭa*) and smeared them all over with cloth-clay (*vastramṛttikā*), one should fill the previously prepared pit with sawdust (*chāṇaka*) and place the pair of saucers into that pit.
Having placed it in the center, fire should be ignited.
Then, when it has become cool, one should again place that same diamond in the middle of a ball of other *vaḍavāikā* plants, ignite it in the same manner, and take out the diamond.
In this way, it should be cooked nine times with nine different *vaḍavāikā* plants, using the young shoots of the royal *badarī*.

Having brought a tender branch and made a hole in it, having placed asafoetida (hiṅgu) both below and above that [hole], and having cast that very diamond into the middle of the hole, having covered it with cloth and clay, one should first cook it in a pit filled with dried cow-dung.
Then again, having thrown a diamond into a hole in the sprout of a jujube branch, he should be cooked in that same manner in the pit.
In this manner, that very diamond should be cooked nine times with fresh sprouts from the branches of the *rājabadarī* tree.

Then, having made a hole in the middle of a large lump of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), one should place that very diamond inside, cover the opening with asafoetida, and place a layer of black gram (*māṣa*) on top; thereafter, having placed that asafoetida-lump into a vessel filled with oil,
fire should be kindled beneath it.
Then once again, in a fresh piece of asafoetida, it is exactly the same.
In this manner, that same diamond should be cooked nine times with nine fresh pieces of *nesahiṅgu* (*khoṭa*).
Having ground that diamond with *thūthāviḍa*, the diamond should be gradually digested (*jāraṇīya*) in the previously mentioned liquid.
This is the first [method], the digestion of diamonds using food and medicinal substances.
START *Rasārṇava* 1.288–291 (The digestion of diamonds by means of food and medicinal substances [2]):
One should collect all the impurities from the ears of female buffaloes.
And with those, the wise one should wrap diamonds that grant prosperity and are of noble origin.
Having placed that [substance] among yams and small tubers, and having wrapped it with cloth and clay,
one should apply a *puṭa* seal on the ground resembling a cock.
Time and again, one should provide packets made from the impurities of the ears, small tubers of the suraṇa, and fresh clay from the laundry. Radhy 1.290.

And by means of twenty-one applications using *kukkuṭaka* and *puṭa* methods on the ground, wise men easily produce diamonds and *annapatha* [medicinal substances]. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* By means of twenty-one cycles of heating (*vār*) in the earth using *kukkuṭaka* and *puṭa* techniques, diamonds and *annapatha* are produced with ease by the learned. (Note: *Kukkuṭaka* refers to a specific type of crucible or heating method shaped like a rooster; *puṭa* refers to a sealed vessel or furnace for smelting; *annapatha* refers to a class of medicinal substances used as tonics).

Having taken the ear-wax of female buffalo and wrapped it around high-quality diamonds, one should then make holes in *sūraṇa* tubers, insert those diamonds encased in the wax into them, coat them all over with cloth and clay,
and place them on the ground in a "cock's nest" (a mound shaped like a hen's roost).

Then, having again taken a diamond and wrapped it in the same manner with the earwax of a buffalo, one should place it inside a *sūraṇa* or small tuber, smear it all over with clay from a cloth, and place it on the ground in a heap of dried cow-dung like a chicken’s nest.

In this manner, wrapping [the substance] twenty-one times with buffalo ear-wax, placing small *sūraṇa* roots within them, and providing hen’s nests upon the ground, one should prepare the "diamonds for food. This is the second procedure for making diamonds into edible food.
START *Rādhya* 1.292–294 (*Vajra*: Preparation for Eating):
One should roll out the soft leaves of that plant which crushes the earth.
Having cast diamonds into that lump, fashion it into a ball. Radhy 1.292.
Having placed it in a hollowed-out leaf-cup and wrapped it with clay from a wall or a rag,
the sealed packet should be buried in the ground in a shape resembling a cock.
Fresh and fresh items should repeatedly be offered in all sixty-four compartments;
indeed, only cocks should be given, and diamonds should be made into the path of food.
*Radhy 1.294* *Commentary: Rasādhyāyaṭīkā*

Having rolled out the tender leaves of the *bhūmyāmardakī* (earth-crusher) or *bhūmiphodī* (earth-breaker), having formed them into balls, having placed genuine diamonds in their centers, and having made them into spheres, one should place them inside a pair of earthen saucers (*śarāva*), apply cloth-and-clay (*karpaṭamṛttikā*) to the seam, and place [the assembly] on the ground in a "cock-pit" (*kurkuṭapuṭa*).

Then again, in the same manner, having thrown diamonds into the middle of a mass of *bhūmyārdakī* plants, having formed them into balls, having placed them in a pair of earthen saucers (*śarāva*), and having applied a clay seal over the joint with a piece of cloth, a "cock-burial" (*kurkuṭapuṭa*) should be performed in the ground.

In this manner, by means of sixty-four "cock-pits" (kurkuṭapuṭas) of earth prepared with fresh balls of *ardhakī* leaves and clods, those diamonds should be placed upon the ground and the paths for the food [of the worms] should be prepared.
This is the meaning. RadhyT 1.292–294:4.
They become cooked like grains of rice and are digested along with the taste.
Thus ends the third rule regarding the construction of a path for diamonds and food.
START Radhy 1.295–303 (Hīrakabhasmīkaraṇa [1]):
It is not burned by fire, nor is it broken, nor is it destroyed by heavy blows.
For when he is submerged in water, he cannot indeed be tested.
Having thrown a toy ball and twenty diamonds into his hands, they should be crushed by both his hands; those which do not lose their brilliance [should be known as authentic]. (Vajra:: Māraṇa, 1.296)
Those diamonds in which not even a single line is present are known as being of pure birth.
Having brought a baked earthen pot, one should fashion numerous cavities within it. (Radhy 1.297)

One should throw high-quality iron pieces into them; then, having repeatedly blown [the fire] until it becomes the color of a flame, those who know the craft should fashion a crucible from it using the materials of the dead.
Human urine and *thauhara* milk, mixed together in equal parts, should be used to repeatedly blow upon the heated crucible with those two. (Radhy 1.299)
Then, having made cavities in new earthen vessels and placed diamonds within them, one should blow upon them;
once they have been blown, one should sprinkle them with a mixture.
Having blown [the bellows] seven times according to this method, one should repeatedly extinguish it;
such [results] as jambūla fruits would appear at the first blowing, and at the second.
In the third [stage] they are lusterless; in the fourth, triangular and circular;
in the fifth, the chāṇikās are fragmented, and diamonds are certainly shattered. Radhy 1.302.
In the sixth stage they are rubbed with the hands; in the seventh, they are broken up again;
then, having been reduced to ashes, those ashes are to be thrown into the *kumpaka*.
*Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):*
This diamond is not burned by fire, it does not break when struck by hammers, and it does not sink in water; for this reason, a diamond is difficult to examine.
Nevertheless, the examination is set forth.

First, having placed one diamond in the hands, and then having released twenty diamonds from the hands, those diamonds should be rubbed with both hands; among them, those diamonds which are not devoid of luster and in which there is not even a single line are genuine diamonds.
The remaining [factors] are non-arisen (*ajāti*).

Then, having brought a fired earthen bowl (karpara), having made several small cavities therein, having placed diamonds within them, and having heated that diamond-filled bowl with *līhālaṅka* until it becomes the color of fire, one should extinguish the fire with human urine and the milk of *yohara* mixed in equal parts; thus the diamond is refined.
In this manner, diamonds should be cooked seven times with fresh crucibles each time.
And therefore, in this case, during the first turn, the diamonds are exactly like that.
On the second day they become emaciated; on the third day they lose their luster.
On the fourth day they are round; on the fifth day they are cut, being severed by a knife.
On the sixth day, those crushed by the hand break apart.
On the seventh day, it takes the form of ashes; then, having cast those ashes into a water-pot, one should release them.
Thus ends the first [chapter], on the reduction of diamonds to ashes.
START *Radhy* 1.304–308 (*vajra*:: *māraṇa*) Haritāla, known as *gandhakāmala-sāra*, and *manaḥśilā* [are used].
The fourth, *suvarṇamākṣika*, should be made in equal proportions.
Having ground four [substances] with water, they should be made into pills resembling the color of lac;
one should apply thick flowers from Puṣpālī to Nisāhā. (Radhy 1.305)
Then, having made a ball of flour and having placed genuine diamonds in its center,
one should form it into a globe and place it inside a diamond-crucible.
One should repeatedly cast that bellows, which has been heated until it glows with the color of fire, into the middle of the *rāva*;
in this manner, the procedure should be performed for fourteen days.
Without effort, the diamonds will undoubtedly be reduced to ashes;
having turned them into powder, the wise one should cast it into a water-jar.
*Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):*
Āmalasāraka is sulphur.
Haritāla, manaḥśilā, and suvarṇamākṣika.
Having mixed these four ingredients in equal proportions and ground them with water, one should fashion them into a mass resembling lac.
Then, having arranged many flowers in a floral pattern upon a *nisāhā* leaf, one should form a ball, place diamonds in its center, and shape it into a spherical lump.
Having placed that sphere inside a diamond crucible (*vajramūṣā*) and heated it until it glows like fire, [one should cast it] into the previously prepared lac.
Having repeatedly cast [the substance] into the crucible, one should blow it out with a bellows.

Then, having again placed those diamonds within a lump of *khāpara* (calamine) and having cast them into a *vajramūṣā* crucible, one should blow [the fire] and cause them to be processed within a *rābā*.
In this manner, one should cook the diamonds with nine different medicinal herbs fourteen times; then the diamonds will easily turn to ash, and that ash should be thrown into a *kumpa* (pot).
Thus ends the second [chapter], on the reduction of diamonds to ash.
START *Radhy* 1.309–312 (*vajra*:: *māraṇa*):
[One should apply] the juice of *ketakī* flowers to the breasts at night without water.
Having stirred it, the juice should be taken, for once purified by a cloth, it is indeed stainless.
With this juice, a fine coating of realgar (manaḥśilā) should be applied;
having wrapped the vajras with it, one should place them inside a vajra-crucible. Radhy 1.310.

Having blown it out and then rekindled it with the milk of the *arka* plant until it has become like fire, this procedure should be performed repeatedly in this manner seven times by one who so desires. (Radhy 1.311)

The six types of diamonds die [in the crucible] and are certainly easy to process; that powder, produced from dead diamonds, should be thrown into the *kumpā* [crucible]. *Rasādhyāyaṭīkā* (Commentary on the Chapter on Mercury): The six types of diamonds are those which, when placed in the crucible, undergo dissolution and are thus easily processed; it is certain that they are "dead" [rendered inert]. That powder, originating from such dead diamonds, must be cast into the *kumpā*.
The juice of *ketakī* stalks should be extracted by wrapping them tightly in a cloth while they are still fresh and squeezing them, even without water, and then filtering it through the cloth.

Then, having prepared realgar with that liquid and wrapped diamonds in it, one should place them inside a diamond crucible; having heated that crucible with fire until it becomes the color of fire, one should extinguish it with the milk of the *arka* plant.
Then, once again, having wrapped the diamonds with realgar processed with the juice of *ketakī* buds,
one should place them in a diamond crucible, heat them, and extinguish the fire with the milk of the sun-plant (*arka*). When this is repeated seven times,
the diamonds are reduced to ashes.
Thus ends the third [chapter], on the reduction of diamonds to ashes.
START *Radhy* 1.313–316 (*vajra*:: *māraṇa*):
One should burn the roots of those *mandāra* and *arka* plants that are white.
While they are being set on fire, those who live off the dead must perform their duties.
In those [spots] that have not been smeared, one should diligently dig pits;
having placed vajras within them, one should cast gold into the fire-altar.

Having smelted excellent vajras with fire using *āmbilya*, *auli*, and *babula* wood—plants that sustain life through nectar—one should cast them into a decoction of horse gram (*kaulattha*). (Radhy 1.315)

Then, by means of that method, those wise ones shall easily kill the diamonds; however, the ashes of the cloths and the powder should be thrown into a water-jar. *Commentary: Rasādhyāyaṭīkā:* By that aforementioned method, the wise ones shall easily reduce the diamonds to ash; this ash, along with the powder of the burnt cloths, is to be cast into a jar.
In this case, having burned the roots of the white *āka* and *madāra*, lead-lacquers (*līhālaka*) are to be prepared.

Then, having carefully made pits in those crucibles (*lihālaka*), and having cast diamonds (*vajra*) into those pits, one should place them in a fire related to gold (*suvarṇasambandhin*), [using] *āmbilī* and *aulibabūla*. Blowing with crucible-blowing pipes (*līhālaka*) until it is equal to fire, one should cast *kulathī* beans into the midst of the boiling liquid and extinguish the fire. By this method, even diamonds are easily reduced to ashes. Thus ends the fourth [section], the reduction of diamonds to ashes.
START *Radhy* 1.317–320 (*vajra*:: *māraṇa*):
One should bring together the roots conjoined with fire from the mouth and the anus.
One should grind śrīkhaṇḍa and smear it upon them along with half [the amount] of clarified butter.
Having placed a diamond of noble quality into a crucible made of *vajra* within the midst of the waves,
and having added half of the remaining *śrīkhaṇḍa*, one should place the crucible upon the fire-brick.
Having blown [the furnace] and made it resemble the primordial fire, one should dissolve [the substance] with "vajra-milk";
then, by this skillful means, even the finest diamonds are easily killed.

Into that water-pot (kumpaka), for their sake, the wise one should throw the powder; the efficacy of the rite performed with diamond-ash (vajrabhasman) will manifest hereafter. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* The wise one should place the powder intended for them into that water-pot; the power of the ritual action performed with diamond-ash will become evident in the future.

Having collected the roots of the *ihāmukhā* plant together with their bark, one should place them inside a crucible along with the residue of *śrīkhaṇḍa*. After placing that crucible upon fire-bricks and blowing it with fire, it should be poured into the milk of the *thohara* plant.
By this method, diamonds are easily reduced to powder.
And one should cast the ashes of those who have died into a water-pot.
The ritual procedure involving this diamond ash and its specific power will be explained further on.
Thus ends the fifth [chapter], on the reduction of diamonds to ashes.

Then, having removed that crucible from the fire-bricks, it should be blown with charcoal.
Likewise, having melted in the crucible as much of the gold streak as there is [in the sample], one should cast it into the middle of the mercury contained within the diamond-crucible.
Then, it becomes a *ṣoṭa* that pierces a thousand [leaves]; and that is to be collected.

Likewise, one thousand *gadyāṇas* each of silver (*tāra*), copper (*tāmra*), and— by the word "etcetera"— tin (*vaṅga*), having been melted separately in a crucible, are each placed individually into the midst of all the lead that has been pierced a thousand times; thus, all the silver and other metals become gold separately.
Thus end the rites concerning the second transformation of fragrant oil.

Having finely ground the best of all salji (sajī) salt, one should place one *maṇa* of it and one jar of water in a pot at twilight; then, in the morning, having discarded the water that has settled, one should take the clear water and pour it over the *salji* salt.

In this manner, having cast six *maṇas* of mercury over six days into a solution of *nīvāra* grain and alkali (*sajjīkṣāra*) water, making it extremely clear, one should grind it with *āmalasāra* and sulfur using that water until it becomes like water. Having placed it in a jar, wrapped it with cloth and clay, applied a layer of mica-paste (*abhrakacātikā*) on the mouth, and covered it with a leaf-lid (*patraculhaka*), a fire burns for a day and night; then, having poured [the liquid] into a ladle (*culūka*).
A protection measuring six finger-breadths all around should be provided; having placed *kumkuma* there, it should be left for twenty-one days and then extracted.
And after that much time, the sulphur, having been stirred within the vessel together with the alkali of *sājī* and having drunk the water, becomes like coconut water.
And this perfumed water, known by the name *Hṛtpīṭhī*, should be understood as being renowned in the midst of the *Vārttikendra*.
START Radhy 1.365–374 (Mercury::
Ṣoṭa): Having ground four *vallas* of purified mercury for two *ghaṭīs*, [one should proceed].
By that yellow water, the mercury is reduced to ashes.
One should produce leaves of pure silver and smear them with this [substance];
then one should heat them in a vajra-mūṣā crucible using a blow-pipe and a bellows.
The silver [coin] became black; it consisted of eight *gadīyāṇakas* combined with as many (twelve) excellent gold *gadīyāṇakas*.
Twenty parts of filtered gold would become twenty-one parts in color;
having cast pure mercury into a crucible, one should apply a gentle fire from below. (Radhy 1.368)
For twenty-one days, one should maintain a mild fire day and night,
repeatedly adding only a single drop of water to the natural sulfur.
Pure mercury, however, [requires] one day and night for twenty-one days;
thus the binding is accomplished, and the mercury becomes sixteen-fold.

Gently roll out the leaves of *pātāla* with a heavy hand; having placed sixteen parts of that which has been ground into a paste within a ball (*piṇḍī*), a globule (*golaka*) should indeed be prepared. (Radhy 1.371)
Having placed it in a clay bowl and wrapped it with a mixture of clay and rags from a seam,
one should apply a seal (puṭa) upon the ground known as "the cock."
With smokeless, glowing embers, the crucible became yellowish in color;
sixty-four gadyāṇas of pure silver were to be melted down.

In the midst of that, when sixty-four *gadyāṇas* have been cast, there shall be excellent gold; this is the *gāndhikī* flux, a *pīṭhī* capable of penetrating [the metal] sixty-four times. *Rasādhyāyaṭīkā*: [Commentary on the above verse: The *gāndhikī* flux is described as follows: one part of mercury (*rasa*) and two parts of *śilājatu* (bitumen) are ground together with *mātuluṅga* (citron) juice. This is placed inside a crucible (*puṭa*) and heated over a fire for three days. When it becomes red, it is called *gāndhikī*. It is used in the process of *vedha* (penetration/transmutation). By means of this *gāndhikī*, one attains the state of a *siddha*. It is said that by using this *gāndhikī*, one can transmute base metals such as copper and lead into gold. Furthermore, it is stated that if one takes this *gāndhikī* and rubs it onto the tongue, one will become invisible to others. It is also taught that if one consumes this *gāndhikī*, one will attain longevity and freedom from disease. Thus, the *gāndhikī* flux is a highly efficacious substance for alchemical transmutation and the attainment of siddhis.
If four *vallās* of purified mercury are cast into sulphur-water for two *ghaṭīs*, they then turn to ash.
Then, having smeared sheets of pure silver with that ash, one should strongly blow upon those sheets in a diamond crucible using a bellows made of tin and melt them.
From that, silver becomes black.

Then, eight *gadyāṇas* of black silver and twelve *gadyāṇas* of the finest new gold—both together amounting to twenty *gadyāṇas*—are melted, and the resulting gold becomes fifteen-carat (*pañcadaśavarṇika*).
Likewise, one should place pure mercury in a crucible and kindle a mild fire beneath it.
One should sprinkle drops of scented water from above, drop by drop.
In this manner, having been sprinkled continuously with sulphur-water for twenty-one days, the well-refined mercury becomes fixed, bound, and rendered stable.

Then, having rolled out the wings of the Pātāla-garuḍa and formed them into a ball (*piṇḍī*), one should place the *ṣoṭa* within that ball and apply a crucible (*puṭa*) known as "cock" (*kukkuṭa*) upon the ground. When this is done with smokeless, glowing charcoal, that *ṣoṭa* becomes liquefied. Then, having melted sixty-four *gadyāṇas* of pure silver and casting the *ṣoṭa*-gadyāṇa into the middle, it becomes the most excellent gold.
For this seat of the mercury-elixir of fragrance (gandhakadrutipīṭhī) exists as that which pierces through sixty-four [levels].
Thus end the procedures for the liquefaction of sulfur and the preparation of the crucible.
Now, the purification of talaka (copper sulfate).
START *Rasārṇava* 1.375–383 (*Haritāla*:: purification):
First, cause the leaves of *godantī* to be applied to the *haritāla*.
As long as they have not become two-fold, one should then place them in a swinging apparatus (dolāyantra).
A vessel filled with stone powder should be used to make it firm; likewise, in a swing-contrivance (dolāyantra), the cloth should be made so that it does not stick to the vessel. Radhy 1.376.
The expert should apply sudorifics with the fire of *haṭha* for two watches;
at the conclusion of the sudorific treatment, one should likewise wash with water.
Just as blue, yellow, black, and other colors emerge from them,
one should always cast objects dried by the sun into a swinging machine.
Furthermore, those [substances] should be sweated in each and every apparatus for two *praharas*;
then, by means of the technique of *luṇa* using a tube, one should sweat them twice more.
Then, one should sweat [the ingredients] in milk and so forth in that sequence;
having cut the *kuṣmāṇḍa* into pieces, one should sweat it with its own juice.
One should roll them with an assistant, using a mare’s milk along with fire;
then one should steam those very fine, sandalwood-shaped [pieces] with that juice. Radhy 1.381.
When purified by the five cleansing agents, the *godaṃtī* plant becomes free of poison;
otherwise, due to impurity, it causes moisture in the heart and produces vomiting. (Radhy 1.382)

It causes heat, constriction of the channels, and internal burning; therefore, it must first be thoroughly purified, becoming like the nectar of yellow orpiment. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* It produces heat, contraction of the vessels, and internal fever. For this reason, it should be purified beforehand, so that it becomes comparable to the nectar of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*).
The leaves of yellow orpiment should be processed in cow's urine until they split into two pieces.

Then, having heated those leaves in a vessel filled with stone powder using a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) over a fierce fire for two *praharas*, they should be subjected to *sveda* (steam-baking).

Then, having removed them and washed them with water, dried them in the sun, and heated them again in a vessel filled with *kāñjika* (fermented rice gruel) mixed with salt using a *dolāyantra* over a fierce fire for two *praharas*, they should be subjected to *sveda*.
Having removed them once more and rinsed them with water, one should steam them for two *praharas* in a vessel filled with cow’s milk or similar milk.
Then, having washed it with water and dried it in the sun, one should cut the fruit of the *kuṣmāṇḍa* into pieces and subject them to steaming for two *praharas* as before, using its juice.

Then, having washed it with milk and dried it in the sun, one should grind it with *vaḍavāṅgā* and *nisāhā*, and steam it for two watches (*yāma*) with that juice as before. Thus, through these five purifications, purified yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) becomes free from poison.
And as long as it is not purified, once it has been given away, it causes distress of the heart, fuming, burning, constriction of the channels, and internal fever.
Therefore, having been purified previously, she becomes equal to nectar.
Thus ends the procedure for purifying godantīharitālā (orpiment from cow-horns).
Now, the procedures for the pure tālaka [pigment].
Take four parts of pure mercury and twenty parts of pure calamine.
Having repeatedly cast goat fat into half a *pala* [of the substance], [one should cook it]. // Radhy 1.384 //
Having ground twenty-four gadyāṇas in a mortar for one day, place them all in a small jar, covering the opening with a shallow earthen bowl. (Radhy 1.385)
Having offered the cloth, one should smear the water-pot with clay from the cloth;
having wrapped it seven times up to its neck, one should place it inside the oven.
A new hearth should be made high and wide enough so that it appears like a swing-mechanism, such that half of the pot rests upon the hearth. (Radhy 1.387)
Half a *kuṃpaka* and one *yāma* of mild fire should then be applied;
thereafter, the fire should be kindled with force until four *yāmas* have passed.
The mercury, having flown upward, will adhere to the neck of the crucible;
then, having broken that crucible, it should be taken out from the neck in its entirety.
Having cast half a *palika* of *sthālī-vasā* into it every moment,
one should grind it daily for seven days and place it in a new vessel.
The previously prescribed procedure should be performed with seven jars in seven ways;
then, at the seventh stage, the thorn attains blackness.
Those drops of water that remain even when the jar is tied up,
as well as all those that have become sentient beings, are to be grasped as being devoid of purposeful activity.
Then, having weighed out twice as much pure mercury from that [quantity],
one should grind it for one *yāma* in two mortars with the juice of *nimbu* (citron).
And the nimba juice should be added repeatedly during the rubbing;
then that pedestal is produced from mercury and talaka.
Having placed that paste in a pot along with sour gruel mixed with salt,
slices of lime, and sugar-candy, one should steam it for a day.
The fermented gruel (kāñjika) mixed with salt should be discarded repeatedly as it is lost;
and that medicinal paste (pīṭhī), once removed from the heat, should be dried in the sun until it becomes firm.
One should grind that *pīṭhī* together with an equal amount of *ṭaṅkaṇa* alkali;
having made two fish-shaped cakes (*mīṇapūpa*), one should place the *pīṭhī* into one of them. Radhy 1.397.
And having placed a second [layer] on top, the wise should fashion a casing;
for as much as that pedestal weighs, so much is pure silver.
One should drain [the liquid] in a vajra-crucible and throw the *veḍhanī* on top;
when the *ṭaṅkaṇa* alkali is burnt and the crucible has become firm, [it is complete]. (Radhy 1.399)
The alloy of copper and silver (ṣoḍaśa) should be like a white conch shell;
one should melt sixty-four gadīyāṇakas of copper alone. Radhy 1.400.
If a *ṣoṭa* coin is dropped into the midst of that [silver], it will certainly become silver;
this *tāla*-silver *ṣoṭa* has a thickness (*pravedha*) of sixty-four [units]. (Radhy 1.401)
Whoever, having risen every morning, practices this for merely a moment daily, even the eight or ten types of leprosy shall perish within six months. (Radhy 1.402)

New teeth emerge and the hair becomes black; grayness departs from the roots and the destruction of wrinkles will certainly occur. (Radhy 1.403) *Commentary: Rasādhyāyaṭīkā:* The emergence of new teeth and the blackening of the hair are signs of rejuvenation. Furthermore, the disappearance of graying from the roots of the hair and the certain destruction of wrinkles indicate the restoration of youth.

Take four *gadyāṇas* of pure mercury and twenty *gadyāṇas* of pure talc; having thus placed these twenty-four *gadyāṇas* into a mortar (*khalva*), add half a *pala* of *chālīvasā*, grind them together for one day, and then place the entire mixture into a crucible (*kuṃpaka*). Cover its mouth with a lid (*karpara*) and a layer of clay (*cātikā*), and seal it up to the neck with seven layers of cloth and clay (*karpaṭamṛttikā*).

Having wrapped the *kumpaka* vessel and constructed a crowded, high hearth, it should be placed upon it so that the *kumpaka* appears like a swinging apparatus; first, it should be heated with a mild fire for one *prahara*, and thereafter for four *yāmas* with a forceful fire (*haṭhāgni*).
And at that moment, the being Tālakasattva flies up and clings to the neck of Kumpaka.

Then, having removed the jar from Kaṇṭhaka and taken all of that [substance], one should place it in a mortar and grind it for one day with half a *palika* of *chālī* fat. On the second day, having placed it in a second vessel, smeared it with seven layers of clay and cloth,
and set it upon a crowded, high hearth, the fire should be ignited beneath it as before.

Furthermore, having ground it again with half a *palika* of rice-alkali (*chālīvasā*) in a mortar, one should perform the entire procedure as before— mixing it into the third vessel and [placing it] on the hearth. Then, if it is thus processed seven times using seven vessels, the *kālikā* (black impurity) moves to the neck [of the vessel], and in the body of the vessel there remain drops resembling water.

The *tālaka* (mica) substances, excluding those of the black variety (*kālika*), should be taken. Then, having weighed that *tālaka* substance and added twice its amount of pure mercury (*pārada*), both should be placed in a mortar and rubbed with the juice of *niṃbu* (citron). A cake (*pīṭhī*) should be prepared from the well-heated *tālaka*, and during the rubbing, the *niṃbu* juice should be added repeatedly.

Then, having bound that *pīṭhī* in a cloth and placed it in a vessel filled with salted *kāñjika* (fermented rice water), one should add pieces of *niṃbu* (citron) and subject it to steaming using a *dolāyantra* for one day. As the salted *kāñjika* is consumed, it should be replenished repeatedly. Then, having removed the *pīṭhī* from the steam, one should dry it in the sun and [mix] an equal amount of *ṭaṅkaṇa* alkali with it. Having ground that *pīṭhī*, one should then make two *mīṇapūpa* (fish-cake) balls; having placed the *pīṭhī* inside one cake, [one should place the second over it].
Having applied a covering on top and formed a seal, one then melts pure silver in a vajra-mūṣā crucible to the exact measure of that base plate and pours it over the top of the seal.
Then, when blown strongly from below, the mineral and the alkali of ṭaṅkaṇa are burnt.
A lump of silver becomes a *tāla*.
Then, having melted sixty-four *gadyāṇaka* of pure copper, one *khoṭa-gadyāṇa* is cast into the middle; it becomes the most excellent silver.
This should be known as the sixty-fourfold penetration (*pravedhaka*) of the *tāla*-silver *khoṭa*.
Likewise, for one who rises every day at dawn and performs the *ṣoḍha* [practice] for a period of *rati*, the eighteen types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) are destroyed within six months.
New teeth emerge, the hair becomes black, gray hairs depart, and the wrinkles vanish.
Thus end the operations concerning the locking-bolt.
Now, there are three types of liquefaction for mica (abhraka).

One should nourish *kodrava* and *vyāghramadana* seeds with a handful (*setikā*) of them; from the midst of that flour, one should extract two *māṇaka*s of the finest powder. (Radhy 1.404)
Having poured *kāñjika* into a vessel, one should fill it with water up to the neck;
after seven days have passed, it becomes extremely sour. (Radhy 1.405)
According to this procedure, a second water that is extremely sour should be prepared;
one *maṇa* of powdered white *abhraka* (mica) should be mixed with that water.
Having cast it into a mortar and pounded it, it becomes *dhānyābhraka*.
Then, one should heat that *dhānyābhraka* in water twenty-one times. (Abhra:: druti) 1.407.
Then, having boiled it and dried it again in the sun, there should be resin (rālā), the alkali of ṭaṅkaṇa, salt, and guggulu. Radhy 1.408.
One mana each for the four types of lamps; when combined, they constitute one mana.
There are twenty palas of sesame seeds and twenty guḍya-weights of molasses.
A small plateful of *vallā* seeds, two *karṣas* each of honey and milk, combined with *dhānyābhra*, should be ground together repeatedly. (Radhy 1.410)
Ten *gadyāṇakas*’ worth of cakes should be prepared in great quantities;
having placed one into the *rākṣasa* machine, one should fill it with charcoal. (Radhy 1.411)
When one [portion] has been strained, the wise person should pour in the second;
all [portions] should be strained in succession over the watches [of the night], and once they have cooled to the temperature of one's own body, he should remove them.
Having extracted from among them the flux derived from mica (*abhraka*), by this method one may easily obtain a flux from *dhānyābhraka* as well. (Dhānyābhraka:: Flux) Radhy 1.413.
Commentary on the *Rasādhyāya*:

Having ground one *setikā* of the *kodrava* grains known as *vyāghra* and *madana*, take two *māṇaka*s of very fine powder from that mixture and place them in a vessel; then fill it with *kāñjika* and water up to the brim.
After seven days, it becomes extremely sour. In this same manner, using the remaining two *māṇaka*s, one should prepare water that is exceedingly sour, performing the process each time individually.

Then, having ground white mica powder with that acidic water in a mortar for one *yāma*, and having soaked it in that very water for twenty-one days, one should subsequently dry it in the sun. Then, adding one-fourth part each of the four medicinal substances— resin (*rālā*), borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa-kṣāra*), salt, and *kaṇa-guggulu*— as well as *gadyāṇa*s of sesame seeds;

Take twenty *gadyāṇas* of jaggery (*guḍa*), one *vallapīṭhīpālī*, one *karṣa* of honey (*madhu*), and one *karṣa* of milk. Having combined all these together with *dhānyābhra* (mica-like mineral), grind them repeatedly until they form a paste. Then, having prepared several small cakes (*pūpa*) the size of ten *gadyāṇakas*, place charcoal into a *rākṣasa* furnace and insert one cake.
And when one [mudrā] has dissolved, one should cast the second.
In this manner, all [the vessels] should be strained within a single watch.
Then, having personally removed the cool cakes from among them, the liquefied essence (druti) produced from *dhānyābhraka* should be extracted.
By this method, the liquefaction of *dhānyābhraka* (grain-like mica) occurs even with ease.
Thus ends the first [section] on the liquefaction of grain-sulphur and mica.
Having thrown two *gadyāṇas* of powdered white *dhānyābhraka* (mica) into a measure of milk, one should repeatedly drink *sehula*. Radhy 1.414.
Just as one might throw a fermented liquor into a vat and it flows out elsewhere,
for having drunk that milk again and again, he voids excrement right there.
All that excrement should be collected after many days have passed;
having weighed it, one should add a fourth part of ṭaṅkaṇa alkali.
Having ground that [substance] with clarified butter and honey until it resembles a paste, one should indeed firmly smear the interior of the *tumbī* and *nalī* apparatus with it. (Radhy 1.417)
Having filled it with charcoal,
that downward-facing small jar should be blown for one watch (yāma) by means of a curved-mouthed bellows.
The melting of white mica (*dhānyābhraka*) that has been rendered free of impurities is called *lepaspheṭha*;

this second transformation of mica-melting should be performed by those who know it. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* The melting of mica that has been freed from its coating of impurities is known as *lepaspheṭha*. This is the second transformation of mica-melting, which should be carried out by experts.
Having placed one *pālī* of milk into the middle of two *gadyāṇas* of powdered white *dhānyābhraka*, it is cooked over a slow fire (*sehulaka*).
And that Sehulaka is thrown into the middle of the pit.
Just as [the medicine] does not pass out elsewhere, then again, two *gadyāṇas* of white *dhānyābhra* are placed in the middle and milk is made to be drunk;
in this way, after many days, whenever his feces are discharged through repeated drinking,
all of that is weighed, and with one-fourth of that amount, *ṭaṅkakṣāra* is added to the middle and ground with ghee and honey.
Having prepared a paste similar to that [of the previous one], and having smeared the base of the *tumbī* and *nalaka* apparatus previously described with that paste,
one should blow upon the vessel— the apparatus being positioned upside down— using bellows (*līhālaka*) and a blowpipe (*vaṅkanālī*).
Then that ointment takes on the form of a liquid.
Thus ends the second transformation: the liquefaction of *dhānyābhra* (grain-like mica).
START *Rasārṇava* 1.420–426 (*dhānyābhra* :: *druti*):
By those wandering [in meditation], a dead hare is seen somewhere through the power of their state of being.
And indeed, the black [spot] should be grasped from the very center of his head.
One should grind forty *gadyāṇas* of *dhānyābhraka*;
then, having added a quantity of powder equal to a *mecaka* from among those, one should place it into the *mecaka*.
Having repeatedly kneaded the two together and then formed them into a firm ball,
one should smear it with ghee, oil, and so forth, and place it into a cooking pot.
A straight, firm, and seamless *ḍhaṅkaṇī* (grinding stone) should be provided, made smooth with clay;
it should be placed within the compartment for the *kaṇīs*, and [the teacher] says that it should be used twenty-one times. 1.423.
Worms are born within it and constantly devour the mica;
and when heated until its dark-blue luster vanishes, they die of hunger.
When all [the other methods] have failed, the remaining process is the liquefaction of grain-sulphurated mica;
this is known by the experts as the third transformation, the liquefaction of grain-sulphurated mica.
The three well-known methods are established; a fourth is not possible.

Now, those actions which belong to the three [methods] shall be explained. *Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* The three well-known methods are established; a fourth is not possible. Now, those actions which belong to the three [methods] shall be explained.
If a rabbit that has died of its own accord is found by those wandering about,
then one should take the black pigment from the middle of its head and grind it thoroughly with forty *gadyāṇas* of *dhānyābhra*. From that,
having added a quantity of powder equal to the black pigment and mixing the two together, one should form a ball and place it inside a dish smeared with either clarified butter or oil.

Having cast the *piṇḍa* [of mercury] inside and placed a lid (*ḍhaṃkaṇī*) upon it, having made it completely seamless on all sides with cloth and clay, that vessel should be placed in the middle of a crucible (*kaṇakoṣṭa*) and kept there for twenty-one days. During that time, worms arise within the *mecaka* [mercury]; they consume the mica (*abhraka*), and subsequently die from hunger and heat.
Then, when those worms have died, that which remains there is repeatedly processed; this is the liquefaction of *dhānyābhraka*.
Thus ends the third transformation: the liquefaction of mica using grain.
In the process of liquefying mica (*abhraka*), there are exactly these three methods.
Now, their ritual actions will be described.
START *Rasārṇava* 1.427–438 (*Mercury*:
*mukhakaraṇa*): Ten *gadyāṇas* of pure mercury [should be placed] inside a diamond crucible (*vajramūṣā*).
Having placed it in a sand-press, one should kindle a gentle fire for a day.
If one repeatedly casts a drop produced from earth, snake, and living being [into the mouth] day and night,
the mouth of the mercury (sūta) will be formed, and everything given [to it] will be digested.
In Niśāhā, one should grind the extremely subtle *cilhā*; having pressed it, the juice should be taken, purified by a cloth and completely free of impurities. (Vajra-Ṣoṭa, 1.429)
Into a beautiful vessel that holds exactly one *pala* of water, ten *gadyāṇakas* of mercury that has just emerged from the mouth [of the crucible] should be placed. (Radhy 1.430)
One should add ten *gadyāṇas* within the interval between three melted substances;
then, one should take a bronze vessel (*kāṃsapātra*) filled with water up to its neck (*ākaṇṭham*). Radhy 1.431.
And one should place that vessel made of magnetic iron (kāntāyasa) in a sand-bath apparatus (vālukaka-yantre);
for a day and night, one should repeatedly ignite a mild fire beneath it.
This wonderful *vajra-ṣoṭa* is produced by the unification of the two;
having cast that [tin] into the *vajra-mūṣā* crucible, the wise one should blow it with charcoal. (Tin = silver) Radhy 1.433.
Having cast twenty gadyāṇas of pure silver into [the crucible],
one should melt it very thoroughly and subsequently draw out the molten metal.
That which is named "indestructible" is fiery, substantial, immovable, and exceedingly pure;
yet when it becomes heavy, it is broken, for such is the nature of the *khoṭaka*.
One should melt one hundred *gadyāṇakas* of tin in a *vajra*-crucible;
when sixty *gadyāṇakas* are added to that mixture, it will certainly become silver. (Radhy 1.436)
The process for the liquefaction of mica is threefold; when applied to tin, it results in a penetration of a hundred times its weight.
That man who always takes even a mere grain from the midst of the six metals [attains success]. (Radhy 1.437)
Within six months, he shall become possessed of great luster, stainless, and imperishable;
this *khoṭa* is renowned on earth as that which certainly produces a body of iron.
*Commentary (Rasādhyāyaṭīkā):* [This refers to the alchemical process wherein the mercury, having been processed, results in an immortal and indestructible state.]

Having placed ten *gadyāṇas* of pure mercury into the middle of a diamond crucible (*vajramūṣā*), one should place that crucible in a sand-bath apparatus (*vālukāyantra*) and apply a mild fire for one day.
One should repeatedly cast drops upon the head of the Bhūnāga-sattva.
From that, the mouth of the essence is born.
Everything given away is digested.
Then, having thoroughly ground the extremely fine *cilha* root of the *nisāhā* plant and squeezed it with a cloth, the juice should be extracted.

Then, having filled a beautiful vessel to the brim with as much water as can hold one *pala*, and having placed that beautiful vessel upon a sand-furnace (*vālukāyantra*), one should apply a mild fire from below repeatedly for a day and night;
thereafter, through the unification of the flux of mica (*abhraka*) and mercury, a mica-crust (*abhraṣoṭa*) is produced.
Then, having placed that *ṣoṭa* into a diamond crucible (*vajramūṣā*), having cast twenty *gadyāṇas* into its midst, and having melted it thoroughly, one should take it out.
Then this [arrow], inexhaustible, stainless, radiant, and wielded by the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, is discharged.
It becomes the most excellent silver.
This is that mercury which, when processed with a hundredfold [additives] in Vaṅga, is a penetrator (vedhaka); likewise, it always produces only a small amount of pleasure at dawn.
Within six months, his body becomes imperishable and free from disease; such are the three methods for the liquefaction of mica (*abhraka*).
Now, the Bhūnāga [mudrā].
START *Radhy* 1.439–458 (Mercury: like the mouth of a Rākṣasa):
A wise person should melt four excellent gold *gadyāṇa*s.
One should have their petals fashioned like the petals of a lotus flower.
One *pala* produced from a human skull, one *pala* born from the root of *dhattūra*,
and sandalwood— having ground each separately, they are mixed together in equal parts.
One should cast one *gadyāṇa* of diamond-ash into the midst of the *śrīkhaṇḍa* and grind it in a mortar until it attains a state of oneness.
One should coat the very firm gold leaves with that same [substance], and one should place a *gadyāṇa* weight of the essence derived from *bhūnāga* into a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*). (Radhy 1.442)
Having cast gold leaves into that very crucible as desired,
it was repeatedly filled to the brim with the fire from a furnace in deep pits.
One should cause it to be blown into a curved-mouthed bellows by those who have revived the dead;
the resulting substance, consisting of gold and diamond, is born from the essence of *bhūnāga*. (Radhy 1.444)
Having heated that *ṣoḍa* [substance], one should make it into a very fine powder;
then, one should coat a glass flask up to its neck seven times with cloth-clay (*vastramṛtsnā*).
Having wrapped it, one should first place one *karṣa* of *bhūnāga*-derived essence (*satva*) in the middle of that, and within that, pure mercury.
Then one should give six *gadyāṇas* [of mercury] and place it in a sand-filled vessel;
having set that vessel upon a stove, one should fiercely kindle a fire beneath it. (Radhy 1.447)
The semen derived from the earth-spirit (bhūnāga) must be discarded again and again whenever it is lost;
furthermore, the small flask (kumpikā) should be filled with and held by means of the fluid essence of semen.
The mercury should be subjected to sweating by a wise person for seven days and nights.
Thus, these six [substances], having been sweated, are considered "sweated" when derived from purified mercury. (Radhy 1.449)

The face of the charioteer became transformed, and the charioteer was born as a Rākṣasa; six gadyāṇas were made from the essence produced by the former golden creeper and other substances. (Radhy 1.450)
From among them, repeatedly casting sixty-fourth parts into the interior of the crucible and grinding them again and again very slowly, one should process [the mixture]. (Radhy 1.451)
These six alone are to be subjected to digestion (jāraṇa); the remaining six are established as born of mercury (sūtajā).
These six excellent gadyāṇas of mercury are to be mixed with these [substances]. 1.452.
By means of *gālī* in a crucible of twelve *mūṣās*, there shall be *ṣoṭa* that pierces a hundred times;
[this applies] to silver, copper, lead, and tin, at the rate of one hundred *gadyāṇas* each. (Gold: Coloring) Radhy 1.453.
When three hundred [units] of each have been melted separately,
one should cast six *gadyāṇas* of that [metal] into each of them individually.

In the three realms, gold is certainly of the color of the lunar day; from the midst of the *ṣoṭa*, one should take a measure of *ratī* at dawn, conjoined with a digit of nectar. (Mercury:: Ṣoṭa:: Administration) Radhy 1.455.
He certainly attains mastery over time; wrinkles do not arise upon him, and gray hair recedes from the roots so that his hairs become black again. Radhy 1.456.
Firmness arises in the body, and the body indeed does not decay;
the luster of the body becomes golden through the constant use of Ṣoṭa. (Radhy 1.457)

Having melted four gold *gadyāṇas* of fifteen *varṇas*, one should fashion leaf-shaped pieces that can be pierced by a thorn, like the petals of the *jarakīśa* flower.

Then, having separately ground *narakapāla* and the root of *dhattūra*, one should combine them in equal parts. Into that mixture, one *gadyāṇa* of previously prepared diamond ash (*hīrakabhasman*) should be added. Then, placing everything in a mortar, one should grind it until it reaches a state of complete homogeneity. Next, having smeared gold leaves with that [mixture] and placed them inside a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), one should add one *gadyāṇa* of *bhūnāga* bark on top and [place it] first in a furnace.
Having filled it with bellows, one should blow upon it through a curved tube.
Then one should blow upon the fire-brick with bellows.
Then, one should blow upon it in a pit using bellows.
Thus, having been blown three times, this mercury—born from gold, vajra, ash, earth, and the best of serpents—becomes ṣoṭa.
Then, having ground that *ṣoḍa* root, a fine powder should be prepared.

Then, having wrapped a glass jar up to its neck with seven layers of cloth and clay, and having placed inside it one *karṣa* of *bhūnāga* mineral as well as six *gadyāṇaka* of pure mercury, one should place that jar in a sand-bath apparatus (*vālukāyantra*) and apply a fierce fire beneath it.
And the *bhūnāgasattva* that has perished must be cast in again.
In short, for seven days without interruption, it must be maintained as if filled by the Kumpikābhūna nāga-sattva.
Just as sixty-five *praharas* [of heating] cause pure mercury to become firmly bound by six *dīnāra*s.

Then his mouth opens, and he becomes a "Sūta" named Rākṣasa, meaning one who eats all things. Then, having previously ground the six-fold essence of gold, diamond, earth, and Nāga, one should take the sixty-fourth part from among that, place it in a mortar together with the Rākṣasa-sūta, and after grinding it again and again, it should be subjected to *jāraṇa* (digestion). Then again, the sixty-fourth part...
In that case, one portion should be ground and subjected to the process of *jāraṇā*.
In this manner, by repeatedly digesting sixty-four parts of *ṣoṭa* at a time, six *gadyāṇas* of *ṣoṭa* are to be digested.

Then, having mixed six *gadīyāṇa* measures of purified, superior mercury with six *gadīyāṇa* measures of [the aforementioned] *rākṣasa-sūta*, these twelve *gadīyāṇa* should be cast into a crucible and melted down.
This results in a *ṣoṭa* that has the power to transmute copper a hundred times its weight (*śatavedhaka*).
Then, having melted a hundred *gadīyāṇakas* of silver, copper, or lead, six *gadīyāṇas* are added [to the mixture].
The gold becomes fifteen-carat.
This elixir is a piercer of a hundred [targets] within the three realms.
Likewise, at dawn, one should regularly take a dose of *ṣoḍhacūrṇa* mixed with a portion of *amṛtakalā*, which produces sexual pleasure.
His defects, such as wrinkles and graying hair, perish.
And his hair becomes black.

This *ṣoṭa*, prepared with gold leaf, vajra-ash, and *nāgasatva*—these three—is a maker of bodies and a maker of iron.
Thus [are described] the rites of gold, vajra, ashes, earth, nāgas, and satvas.

The number eighty-four occurs individually in each of the three;

From the beginning of the undertaking until the end of the fruit, one should perform uninterrupted austerity from among this entire number for any single [deity]. (Radhy 1.461)
Until its completion and even until the fruit is attained, he should remain celibate, sleep on the ground, and eat only sacrificial food (haviṣya). (Radhy 1.462)
In the practices of austerity, those things to be accomplished through austerity, such as the vital essences (rasas), are perfected;
for practitioners devoid of austerity merely attribute their failure to the fault of fate.
The medicinal pills have been described by that venerable yogin Kaṅkālaya;
I shall now describe the pill that bears the fruit of gnosis, consisting of fifty-two excellent stalks.
Four [parts] from abhraka-sattva, four from svarṇamākṣika, four from pure silver, and one *vala* of *hemarājikā*. (Radhy 1.465)
The previous mercury, which has been purified by eighteen refinements, amounts to thirty-nine when combined with fifty-two. (Radhy 1.466)
Having placed all of those in a mortar, one should grind them for seven days,
repeatedly using the fine powder of *śrīkhaṇḍa* from the *varuṇa* tree.
One should subject it to sudation over a mild fire in a *dolāyantra* for two days;
having made that into a pill, one should then subject it to sudation gradually with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
Honey, clarified butter, curd, milk, and sugar as the fifth—these five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are used for steaming [the deity] eight times for each nectar. Radhy 1.469.
One should place the pill in a vessel made of kāntaloha iron along with honey;
then, one should set that vessel inside a pot filled with sand. (Radhy 1.470)
Having placed the vessel on the stove and lit the fire beneath it, one should maintain it for eight watches;
this procedure for steaming should be applied respectively to *stokaka* and *amṛta*. (Radhy 1.471)
Whenever it is lost, one should repeatedly cast in the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in due order; following the method for combining honey, one should always heat the pill five times.
Devoted to austerity and performing the ritual actions, one should roll it with both hands;
when the pill is completed, it should consist of fifty-two folds.

Salutations to Śrī Bhairava, Gaṇādhipati, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī; by whose grace pills, collyriums, and mercurial elixirs are perfected.
In that regard, there are eighty-four (84) medicinal pills, eighty-four (84) collyriums, and eighty-four (84) alchemical operations involving mercury.
Thus, in total, there are two hundred and fifty-two (252) [cases] for the three [categories].

From among these two hundred and fifty-two [substances], for any one of them— whether it be a pill-medicine, a collyrium, or mercury— at the very beginning of its commencement as well as at the conclusion of its fruit, unbroken austerity must be performed.

In that regard, for one month prior to the commencement and likewise for one month until the completion of the rite, one must observe celibacy; as for food, one should eat sacrificial grain (*haviṣyānna*), milk-rice (*paramānna*) mixed with ghee and other ingredients, or milk.
In the performance of austerities, ritual actions attain success.

Since the attainment of the *rasas* and other effects is accomplished through austerity (*tapas*), those practitioners who are devoid of austerity ultimately attribute the failure to the fault or obstacle of destiny (*daiva*).
By that foremost of ascetics, the illustrious Śrīkaṅkālayayogin, this discourse was spoken; the pill described by the one who knows the alchemical process of the elements exists.
From among those, I shall describe the pill which is the fruit of knowledge and the cause of knowledge, prepared from fifty-two *valla*-measurements of medicinal herbs.

In that regard, there are four *vallās* of *abhraka-sattva*, four *vallās* of *svarṇamākṣika*, four *vallās* of pure silver (*śuddharūpya*), and one *vallo* of *hemarāja*. Likewise, of that previously mentioned purified mercury (*pārada*) which has undergone eighteen refinements, there are thirty-nine *vallās*.
Thus, when combined, all [the ingredients] amount to fifty-two *vallās*.
Having placed it in a mortar, one should grind it for seven days.

Having bound all the medicinal herbs in a cloth and placed them in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) within a vessel, one should steam them with that *śrīṣaṇḍa* over a gentle fire for two days; then, having removed them and formed them into pills, one should subsequently steam them in sequence with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
In that context, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) consist of honey, clarified butter, curd, milk, and sugar.
In that regard, this is the procedure for sudation: RadhyT_1.459–478:15.

First, one pill should be placed with honey in a vessel of bell-metal or iron, inside a pot filled with sand; that pot should be set on the stove, and fire should be lit beneath it for eight *praharas*, while honey is poured over the top.

Thereafter, as each portion is consumed, honey must be added again and again; having thus sweated it with honey for eight hours, one should remove it, and then, placing a pill together with clarified butter in a vessel of kāntaloha iron, one should sweat it in a *vālukāyantra* (sand-oven) for eight hours.
Then, in this manner, one should take eight *praharas* with curd, then eight *praharas* with milk, and then eight *praharas* with sugar-water.

Having thus steamed the pill five times with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one who practices austerity and maintains celibacy should wash it with both hands and prepare a pill measuring fifty-two *vallas*. Then, [one should choose] a girl whose maternal and paternal lineages are pure.
Whether she be a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyī born of a most noble family.
Excluding a Śūdra woman, when her first pregnancy occurs, then after one month has passed, that pill should be administered.
And she must wear it continuously for one month, except during the times of eating, taking medicine, chewing betel, and drinking water.

Then, after a month had passed, by the power of the pill, when questioned, that woman spoke forthwith of knowledge concerning the three times—the past, future, and present—producing immediate conviction. The power of this pill is truly most wonderful.
For whatever a knower speaks exactly as it is, all that becomes true.
Likewise, through the power of casting a pill into her mouth, whatever a Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriyā, or Vaiśyā speaks becomes exactly so.

The meaning is that the extraordinary power (*prabhāvātiśaya*) of mercury (*rasa*), *pārada*, medicinal pills (*guṭikā*), as well as collyriums such as *pātālāñjana* and others, is great—that is, it is weighty.
This pill is indeed called "the speaker."

Although its correct traditional transmission is not currently available, nevertheless, the commentary is provided by means of reasoning for some of the literal meaning, through the experience of other medicinal pills for some, and in accordance with such scriptural authority and logic for others.

Thus, having thoroughly understood the eighty-four types of pills (84), the eighty-four types of ointments (84), and the eighty-four varieties of mercury (84), the former Śrīkaṅkālaya-yogin taught a certain essence of mercury for the sake of his own disciples' comprehension, for the sake of ensuring their well-being and security, and for the benefit of all.
